#What changed, round 12: the script stage of DOM-heavy pages, the crossings and the interpreter's exits

Item 1 of round 11's list. Profiled first, as rounds 6 and 7 did: the engine's samples (jspage -image <engine built with buildjs -names> -profile, the guest profiler: a sample at each 5 ms epoch tick, taken where Wasm code checks the epoch, so the time of a call into the browser is counted to the first function the engine enters after it returns: Node_preInsert to JS_DupValue, the factories to the wrapping that follows them, Node_unpinAll to gc_collect), the browser's side under page::run_animation_frames and under _t_dom_Node_preInsert (WREN_SAMPLE_UNDER). Each change was timed in jspage on a copy of nodes10k (build() a frame, p50 of 250 frames; the collection with a timer around js.collect in a build of jspage that was not kept), every engine image of the round in turn in one jspage, 6 rounds; other agents built and ran tests all along, so single runs moved by up to a factor of 2 and the ratios within a round (each build against the first) were read with the medians. Then the browser, all of it (5 runs of each build, interleaved, the order turning).

What the engine's samples of nodes10k were (9 105 samples, the base): the interpreter 22 % of its own (interp_hot 15 %, interp_run 7 %: the full dispatch for what the hot loop gave up on), the browser's insertions 10.5 % (counted to JS_DupValue), the browser's createElement and createTextNode 8.7 % (counted to wj_wrap_node) and Node_wrap 4.5 % (counted to make_wrapper), the collection 9 %, the C API's bridge and its value conversions (enc, dec) 8 %, Odin's append of the engine's root lists 4 %, the two crossings for the realm's document (the document getter and is_page_document) 6.4 %.

  1. A new node and its wrapper in one call (Document_createElementWrapped, Document_createTextWrapped in api/js.widl, src/page/js_host.odin; wj_wrap_new, native/js/odin/wj/qjs_platform.odin). document.createElement crossed to the browser four times (the document getter, is_page_document's Window_document, the factory, Node_wrap for the pin and the interface), createTextNode as many. The realm's own document now makes its node and pins it and names its interface in one call, whose answer (WrappedNode: the node, its interface) is what the wrapper needs; a custom element whose constructor made its wrapper before the call returned keeps that wrapper's pin (the engine drops the extra one). Documents of their own and other pages' documents take the old path. The realm's document asked once (wj_document): its handle never changes under a realm. Every document of a page is made with the page's tag and its document node is the first slot of a fresh pool (dom.document_create), so a document the page adopts (a frame's parsed document after its about:blank, an XML one) has the handle of the one it replaced; the glue already kept the tag it derives from it. window.document is the glue's (wjr_Window_get_document), and is_page_document compares handles. One crossing for each new node where there were four. build() 11.11 (10.93-11.40) -> 10.55 (10.43-15.76) ms. Tests: adopted_document_keeps_its_handle (page: HTML, XHTML, parsed off the thread), js_new_nodes_wrapped_in_one_call (web tests: interfaces, one pin for each wrapper, a custom element constructed during createElement, the browser's errors, the same document object).
  2. The engine's root lists appended in place (list_push, src/engine/jsrt/gc.odin): every cell made goes on temp_roots, every host object of a class with references on gc_hooked, every marked cell on gray; Odin's append is a call that checks the allocator each time, now taken only when the list is full. build() 10.55 -> 10.25 (10.18-10.73) ms.
  3. The hot loop calls native getters and pushes string constants (hot_get_prop, hot_native_getter, get_var, push_atom_value in src/engine/jsrt/interp_hot.odin; global_index, globals.odin). A DOM attribute (list.lastChild), an accessor of the global object (document) and a string constant ("item ") left the hot loop for the full dispatch and came back to it; the getter, a native called as a function, is now called where the lookup found it, as a call instruction calls a native (call_native, the same checks of depth and stack). build() 10.25 -> 9.11 (8.81-10.35) ms.
  4. The C API's bridge converts its values in place (#force_inline enc and dec in bridge_invoke, src/engine/jscapi/runtime.odin): every DOM call converted its this, its arguments and its result through two calls each. build() 9.11 -> 8.73 (8.65-13.32) ms.
  5. The class and the opaque data of a platform object in one call (JS_GetAnyOpaque, QuickJS-ng's, in src/engine/jscapi): obj_of, which every DOM call makes for its this and node arguments, and the collection's obj_mark and obj_finalizer, asked JS_GetClassID then JS_GetOpaque; obj_mark reports a group only when the wrapper is in one. With the gray list of 2: the collection 4.07 (3.89-6.54) -> 3.69 (3.53-4.15) ms (median of the ratios 0.90), build() 8.73 -> 8.60 (8.53-8.85) ms. Test: judge capi (a payload and its class, a built-in object's class and no data, no object).
  6. Measured, not kept. The finalizer of a wrapper skipping the calls for what it does not have (listeners, a group, [SameObject] values): the collection 4.23 (3.89-5.82) against 4.36 (3.89-5.23) ms with it, 8 rounds. The walks of every cell before the sweep (the finalizers', the shapes' transitions) in one: the collection the same (4.03 against 4.03 ms, ratio 1.03), the heap fits the processor's cache. node_next inlined in the prologue: the collection the same (3.99 against 3.99 ms). The shrink of temp_roots at each native call's return written in place (temp_reset, _resize_dynamic_array 2 % of the engine's samples after 1 to 5): build() 8.92 against 8.97 ms, 8 rounds.

#What changed, round 13: the script stage of DOM-heavy pages, the collection

Item 1 of round 12's list. Profiled first: the engine's samples (the guest profiler in jspage, its ticks at 1 ms with --pref wasm.wasmtime.epoch_tick_ms=1: 19 306 samples in 3 000 frames, the bias of round 12), the browser's under each import (WREN_SAMPLE_UNDER=page::[api_generated.odin]::_t_dom_Node_preInsert and the others). The browser's side of nodes10k's script stage is small: a frame spends 0.50 ms in Node_preInsert (journal_record 23 %, its halving's memcpy 6 %, the insertion hooks 29 %, check_insert 9 %), 0.31 ms in Node_unpinAll (destroy_subtree 69 %, unpin 29 %), 0.29 ms in createElementWrapped, 0.15 in createTextWrapped, 0.11 in preRemove: 1.4 of the 12 ms; the rest is the engine. Single calls timed in jspage (a loop of a million, the best of 7): the loop alone 25.5 ns an iteration (the interpreter, the loop JIT does not take a loop that reads a property), a property of the object itself 34 ns, a method of li found on the fifth shape of its chain 54 ns (about 4 ns a shape), the glue's document getter 77 ns, nodeType 104 ns, firstChild 122 ns. Each change was timed in jspage on a copy of nodes10k (build() a frame, p50 of 400 frames; the collection by a timer around js.collect in a build of jspage that was not kept), the builds in turn, 6 to 7 rounds; the engine's changes also against examples/jsbench/micro.js and macro.js (jsengine run, the best of 2 to 4 runs of each case); then the browser (5 runs of each build, interleaved, the order turning).

  1. A wrapper's data asked for its values only once it holds some (host_object_set_marked, src/engine/jsrt/host_class.odin; JS_SetOpaqueMarked, src/engine/jscapi; wj_obj_marked, native/js/odin/wj/qjs_platform.odin). Every wrapper was in gc_hooked, so each collection called its class's gc_mark (the bridge, then the glue's obj_mark) in the counting pass of the trial deletion, and again when marking the live ones: on nodes10k, 20 000 wrappers a collection that hold nothing. An object made with a payload (JS_NewObjectProtoClassPayload) is now unmarked: out of gc_hooked, never asked; the glue marks it before its data takes a value (a group, a listener, a [SameObject] value, an impl), and it stays so. One the glue forgot to mark keeps the values its data counts as roots (their counts are not subtracted): a leak, not an early free. The collection 3.49 (3.42-3.81) -> 3.03 (2.99-3.88) ms; build() the same. A first version that made the wrapper marked and took it out after (JS_SetOpaqueMarked(.., false) in wrap_pinned) saved as much in the collection and cost it back in build() (8.54 -> 8.71 ms). Test: judge capi (gc_mark not called until marked, the counted values roots until then, a cycle through marked payloads collected).
  2. A detached tree freed by its own links (destroy_subtree, src/dom/dom.odin): a node after its children, the walk going down by first_child and on by next or back to the parent; the template contents and shadow trees that go with it, rare, in a list of the temporary allocator. It made a heap list for each tree (2 500 a collection on nodes10k, _reserve_dynamic_array 13 % of Node_unpinAll), and looked a node up in the maps of namespaces and templates when they were empty. The collection 3.08 (2.99-3.17) -> 2.83 (2.79-4.58) ms. Round 6 measured an inline list for the same stack within the noise of its timer; the jspage timer of this round tells them apart. Test: release_frees_deep_trees_templates_and_shadows (a chain of 50 000, siblings, a template's contents and a shadow tree all freed; pinned contents kept, then freed with their last pin).
  3. Measured, not kept: the prototype walk without the host class's hooks (hot_get_prop). A bit of Object (exotic_get, set when the object is made: a proxy, a module namespace, a String object, a typed array, a host object whose class has exotic hooks) in place of the four class tests and the call to host_exotic_of at each shape of the chain: build() 8.73 (8.66-9.17) -> 8.51 (8.46-12.68) ms, but every case of micro.js slower (the int loop, which reads no property, 34 -> 40 ns; the geometric mean +12 %) and macro.js +2.3 %: the code of interp_run around the hot loop changed (the bit declared and set but not read: no change). The same test kept out of line (a #force_no_inline procedure, or in host_exotic_of) slowed micro.js as much and gained nothing on nodes10k. A cache of lookups by shape is what the rules rule out; flattening the chain's shapes would need invalidation when a prototype changes.
  4. Not done, by the samples: the journal's halving (memcpy 0.03 ms a frame: a ring would change the slice journal_since gives its four readers for that); texts on the heap one by one (create_text, freed in free_node_data: about 0.1 ms a frame between the two).

The ::backdrop entries tried for the elements of the top layer alone (Index.backdrop, src/style/engine.odin bucket_add; collect_entries, src/style/cascade.odin; match_element, src/style/sibling_match.odin). Since ::backdrop gets a style, the UA's ::backdrop, :fullscreen:not(:root)::backdrop and :popover-open::backdrop were universal entries matched for every element (the last two own, so matched again for each sibling the walk shares matching with), and every element's ::backdrop list (the UA's first rule) went into its share key, to be dropped by compute_element for an element outside the top layer. They are now in a list of their own, whatever their subject (Tailwind's *, ::before, ::after, ::backdrop too), tried only for an element of the top layer; such an element neither takes a family's matching nor gives its own (its siblings would get or miss its backdrop). The share key and the lists of every other element are those of before ::backdrop. A full pass in process 0.632 (0.624-0.643) -> 0.569 (0.565-0.579) ms; the browser below. Test: backdrop_styles (three alike siblings, each in turn in the top layer: it alone has a backdrop). ::placeholder needs nothing of the kind: the UA's rules are by tag (input, textarea).

#What changed, round 15: the interpreter's hot loop calls nothing; real pages loaded from the navigation

Items 9 and 1 of round 14's list, and pages of the site measured from their navigation. The engine's changes were timed with jsengine run -image <engine> on examples/jsbench/micro.js and macro.js (every engine image of the round in turn in one jsengine, 4 rounds; another agent built and ran tests on the machine all along, so single runs moved by up to a factor of 2: the best run of each case is the figure, the median of the runs said the same within a few per cent), and in jspage -image on a timed copy of nodes10k (build() a frame over 400 frames, 5 rounds: its p50 was bimodal with the machine's load, 8.6 or 14 to 20 ms in every build, so its p10 is the figure); then the browser (5 runs of each build, interleaved).

  1. The hot loop calls nothing (interp_hot, src/engine/jsrt/interp_hot.odin). What round 13 saw, looked at in the code LLVM makes for wasm32 (odin build -build-mode:asm): interp_hot was a procedure of its own with 36 locals and calls in its handlers (call_native three times, frame_push, close_var_refs and the dynamic array's resize of an inlined frame_pop, atom_to_value, host_exotic_of, and shape_realize from each of the seven inlined shape_find). Wasmtime compiles Wasm calls with a convention that saves no register across them, so ip, s and the frame's registers, live across those calls in some handlers, were split or kept in stack slots wherever the register allocator chose, and a change elsewhere in the procedure moved that choice (round 13's bit test). Now every handler that needs a call (call instructions, returns, getters, a lazy shape, an atom's number made a string) is a procedure of its own, never inlined (hot_call, hot_return, hot_get_field, hot_get_var_getter, hot_push_atom), that reads and writes the loop's registers in a Hot in memory: written before the call, read back after it, so no value of the loop lives across one. The loop's lookups read realized shapes only (shape_lookup, shape_find without its realization; a lazy shape goes to hot_get_field or to the full dispatch). The listing of the loop now has calls only to those procedures and to the bounds checks' traps, which do not return. A loop that calls nothing LLVM inlined into interp_run of its own accord (the full dispatch and the loop then share pc and sp without a call); it is now #force_inline, so that does not depend on its size. Built as a procedure of its own (#force_no_inline) the same loop was 8 % slower on micro.js than inlined (0.875 against 0.801 of the base, same runs).
  2. The prototype walk without the host class's hooks, again (Object.host_exotic, src/engine/jsrt/object.odin, set by host_object_new: the class has exotic hooks or was not defined when the object was made). Round 13's change, which then slowed micro.js 12 %: on top of 1, the loop walks a node wrapper's chain to the DOM attribute's getter itself (without it, the loop handed every lookup that met a host object to hot_get_field, build() 8.51 -> 8.81 ms p10); with it, the int loop that reads no property is 0.74 of the base's time against 0.76 without the bit (best runs, two series of the same hour), not slower.

#What changed, round 16: first page loads

Item 10 of round 15's list. The machine quiet but for another agent's test_all during one series (thrown away and run again: the numbers below are the quiet series). The browser: wrentool bench perf, profile builds, 5 runs of each build, interleaved, the order turning; median, range in brackets; times in ms from the navigation's start (the page's Navigation and Paint Timing). The base is master at 5af6e1ec.

  1. The engine's compiled code read ahead, off the window thread (js_read_ahead, src/page/js_realm.odin; wasm.read_ahead, src/wasm/module_cache.odin). The first realm of a process hashed the 7 MB image for its digest (wasm.digest, 3.5 ms), read the disk cache's file and checked its HMAC-SHA256 (disk_load, sha256_transf_hw), had Wasmtime deserialize it and resolved its imports, all on the window thread before the page's first script. Now js_startup starts a thread that does all of it into the module cache's memory (only from the disk: a module not on disk is not compiled ahead, nothing is done when memory keeps no module); the first realm, and the compile threads' engines, wait for it only while it runs (a state in a futex: Off, Running, Done), then find the module in memory. In the samples of nav_js_dom the window thread no longer has cache_acquire nor disk_load. Test: read_ahead_from_disk (wasm: nothing compiled ahead without an entry on disk; read ahead on another thread, the instance made after it reads nothing from the disk and runs).
  2. What waits for a stylesheet goes on when it arrives (arrived_pump, src/page/styles.odin, called when a sheet is in or failed, after an off-thread parse, and once the element events of sheets and images are dispatched). The parser's script that waits for the sheets and the document's load event looked again only at the poll (javascript.load.poll_ms, 16 ms, longer with the loop's timer slices); found in shadow-dom.html, whose sheets were in at 7 to 10 ms (Resource Timing) and whose script ran at 34 to 59. The first paint of such a page now comes after its script (as the specification has it, the script before the rendering): shadow-dom.html's first contentful paint 8.1 -> 13.3 ms for an interactive 59.0 -> 11.9 ms. Test: e2e jsload_a_sheet_in_lets_the_parser_and_the_load_go_on (the poll set past the test's wait: the script runs and the load fires).
  3. Direct2D for color glyphs made ahead (font.color_prepare, toolkit 0.74.0; fonts_color_start, src/browser/fonts.odin). The first glyph of a system color font a frame looked up (is_color_glyph, which asks what Direct2D can draw) made the WARP device and the Direct2D context on the window thread: 20.1 ms of text.html's first paint (timed, once). The DWriteCreateFactory and color glyph formats round 15 saw under platform_color_glyph were that. A thread of its own makes it once the first frame's work is under way, joined before the font state goes. Made on the font preload thread instead (joined before the first present) it cost the first present 10 ms (wrentool bench startup, 4 rounds of 3: 247 against 238 without it): not kept there.
  4. Textures zeroed on the GPU (toolkit 0.74.0, zero_texture in render/render_d3d.odin): a texture is a render target too and is zeroed by ClearRenderTargetView, where its zeros were uploaded: the glyph atlas's R8 page (2048 x 2048, a driver call per row) took 5.8 ms of the start, the first color page (RGBA, in 1 MB bands) 3.5 ms of the first frame with a color glyph (its Submit). Only a format that cannot be a render target is still uploaded.
  5. The thread count of stats walks this process's threads (base.process_threads, src/base/process_times_windows.odin: NtGetNextThread, a handle to each thread of this process in turn). The process snapshot it replaced copied every process of the machine: 19.3 to 20.3 ms a call, against 10 to 12 µs (a process of 4 threads, best of 3); in the samples of nav_index, 17 ms of ZwQuerySystemInformation under m_stats before, none after.   1. Slug's bands made from one sort per axis (toolkit 0.75.0, slug_build, font/slug_build.odin: band_axis, band_grid, band_span). The curves an axis's bands can hold were tested against every band of each of the ten band counts pick_band_count tries (108 bands an axis), then each band of the chosen count tested every curve again and sorted its own list. Now the curves of an axis are sorted once, by a u64 key each (the order of the largest coordinate across the band, inverted, above the curve's index: the lists' order, stable), their extents kept in arrays in that order; a curve's first and last bands come from its bounds times the count, corrected against the bands' own bounds (the same expressions as before, so the same bands); a count's fullest band is the running sum of curves starting and ending; the lists are filled curve by curve in the sorted order. The bounds are read from the half-float texels already written (the conversions are calls: no F16C in the generic x86-64 target). The same data (test slug bands_are_their_definition: 300 glyphs of three faces, the counts and every list against the definition written out); built alone, 400 glyphs: Segoe UI 5.52 -> 2.77 ms, Times New Roman 8.21 -> 3.85, Nirmala UI 9.91 -> 4.56 (the outlines 0.4 to 0.5 ms). In the page: text.html's first paint frame below.
  2. The image decoder's start waits for nothing (decoder_start, codecs_wait, src/images/pool.odin). Starting the pool, at a page's first image, waited on the window thread for its first thread to probe the optional codecs (COM, the imaging factory, HEIF's decoder: 12 ms of samples under page::element_start on legacy-html.html), for <source type> selection; the wait is now in codec_supported(.Heif), the one answer that needs the probe, and the probe's post is given back for the next to ask. That 12 ms was what held legacy-html.html's first paint, not a PNG's decode as round 16 read it (the decoder's threads were busy 1 ms in all): with the window thread taken, its stylesheet's completion (Resource Timing: theme.css 2 -> 41 ms) and then its @import's (42 -> 72 ms) each waited for the next frame, whose time slot came first (below, item 4). Test: optional_codecs_asked_after_the_probe (images: the answer for HEIF after the probe, the probe's).
  3. Measured, not kept: Slug's data made by the thread that shapes a word (slug_prepare from the toolkit's shape_word, built outside the atlas lock and stored under it, color faces and hinted glyphs left to the drawing). The paint's share went (text.html Paint_Items 20.0 -> 8.7 ms) but onto the passes the first paint waits for: text.html's first contentful paint 15.4 (14.6-15.5) -> 38.2 (37.3-56.2) ms (its layout ended past its frame's slot), shadow-dom.html's DOM interactive 12.1 -> 15.6 ms (its script's read of the layout shapes on the window thread), index.html's first contentful paint 9.8 -> 13.2 ms. The data a frame draws is made before that frame whichever thread makes it; only less of it to make helps.
  4. Found, not changed: a frame waits for its time slot before the loop's tasks run. A frame begins with the wait for its slot (pacer_wait: the timer, then the swap chain), and only then runs what arrived (host.run_ready): a task that comes during the wait waits with it. In a run of frames (each task asks for two) a first paint pays it once per hop: p10k's parsed document arrived during the wait of the frame that then styled, laid out and painted it (Wait 15.1 ms of that 44 ms frame), legacy-html.html's sheet and its import one slot each. Running the tasks while the slot is waited for (the wait woken by the loop's own wake-up, the frame started at once when a document's first paint can be made) is item 10 below: it changes when the loop's tasks run against the frame gate and the chrome frames made under scripts, a change of its own.
  5. Measured, not changed: the first realm (round 16's item 10). Since the read-ahead, js-dom.html's and shadow-dom.html's scripts run 5 ms after their response or sheets, the instantiation, the realm's start, the script and the DOM work it does together (3 to 4 samples of 1 ms under page::js_run a load); moving the instantiation to the read-ahead thread (a Wasmtime store may change threads, but the instance's options, owner and scope are the page's) would take a part of that. Not done. p10k's first passes (style, layout, paint: 23 ms in the frame of its first paint, after the 15 ms of item 4) were not changed either; nor the script stage of DOM-heavy pages (item 1).

#What changed, round 18: the frame's wait for its slot runs the loop's tasks

Item 10 of round 17's list, its first part. The browser: wrentool bench perf, profile builds, 7 runs of each build (5 in the first series, thrown away: another agent built on the machine meanwhile, ranges of 30 to 90 ms), interleaved, the order turning; median, range in brackets; times in ms from the navigation's start. The start: wrentool bench startup, 4 rounds of 3, interleaved. The base is master at 96183c0e.

  1. The loop's tasks run while the frame waits for its slot (pacer_slot_wait, src/browser/pacing.odin). A frame began with the wait for its time slot (the pacing timer, then the swap chain) and only then ran what had arrived (host.run_ready in its page phase): what came during the wait waited with it, a slot per hop of a load. Now the first frame of a pass runs the ready tasks and timers in its wait (main.odin frame_tasks, in a page phase of their own, shell_wait_tasks: a long script there is preempted by chrome frames as in the frame's), then waits on the timer armed for the slot or for the loop's next timer, whichever is first; a post from another thread during the wait fires the timer at once (the loop's wake-up, wake_window -> pacer_wake: an atomic flag says a frame waits on it; the timer is armed before the loop is looked at, so a post after that look is never lost). The tasks run once a frame, in its wait or else in its page phase: run in both, the first frame of the browser took what the second one ran before its first present (home_idle's first frame to the first present 22 to 30 -> 41 to 54 ms): not kept. Off Windows the wait stays a sleep (no timer to fire). The frame gate does not change: the tasks run in the frame's Polling stage, where the chrome frames they may make are Light frames the gate admits there (the e2e suite's gate counts no violation). Test: the_loop_tasks_run_while_a_frame_waits_for_its_slot (browser: a post from another thread 20 ms into a wait of 200 ms and a timer of the loop due at 40 ms both run before the slot, and the wait ends at its slot).
  2. A first paint does not wait for the slot (first_paint_due, src/browser/first_paint.odin). When the current tab's document has not painted, waits for no render-blocking sheet or font, and has changed since its last layout or was held by render-blocking resources in the last page phase (Page_Prep.blocked), its frame starts at once: neither the timer nor the swap chain is waited for, and the swap chain may queue two frames for it (it is shown at the next refresh, not torn). The document's own changes alone were not enough: legacy-html.html was laid out before its @import was found, and the import's arrival changes the styles, not the document (its first paint 40.7 ms, as before). A frame started at once that laid the document out and held it (paint holding: nothing contentful yet) lets the next one wait for its slot (Pacer.first_paint_laid): a held page that a script changes is not drawn as fast as the thread goes.

#What changed, round 19: the licence card of about:wren under the pointer

wrentool bench perf -Only card_hover -Shown (about:wren?card=sample, the card scrolled into view, the pointer wandering over it every 8 ms; card_idle: the card at rest), profile builds, 3 interleaved runs, 60 Hz, RTX 4070 SUPER (the hardware adapter: nvwgf2umx.dll in the process, not WARP). GPU times are those of a GPU that the driver keeps at low clocks for so little work: the counts of -GpuSteps 1 say more.

  1. A document changed only in style attributes is refreshed, not laid out (styles_only_mutations, src/layout/refresh.odin). The card's script writes its tilt in the style attributes of the card, its lettering and the seal's shadow at each frame (transform, --rx...): paint-only values, but any change of the document disqualified the refresh path, the incremental pass ran (0.2 ms, nothing to lay out), and the compositor, seeing a layout pass, drew the page directly for render.compositor.settle_ms, without its kept layers: the card's 59 planes (the rims are 52 of them) rasterized again at every frame. #What changed, round 20: the loop JIT takes properties and calls

The loop JIT (src/engine/jsrt/jit.odin, engine/jit.md) compiled loops of number arithmetic, comparisons, branches and locals; a property read, a call or a global kept the loop interpreted (round 13: "the loop JIT does not take a loop that reads a property"). Measured with jsengine run -jit -image <engine> on examples/jsbench/micro.js, macro.js and realworld.js (new: JSON records, particles updated in place, a sort with a comparator, a tokenizer over charCodeAt, methods of a class), every engine image of the round in turn in one round, 5 rounds; other agents built and ran tests on the machine all along, so single runs moved by up to a factor of 2 (a round of the base at twice its time is the machine): the figure is the median of the 5 runs, the range in brackets, and where a series was hit the minimum says the same. The checksums of the three scripts are the same in every build.

  1. Properties (jit_get_field, jit_put_field, jit_global, jit_var_ref, j_prop_addr). A named property read or written is a guard of the object's own shape against the shapes the site was compiled for (a few per site, tried in turn), then the slot at a constant index, in the object or in the prototype that holds it, whose shape is guarded too; a dictionary holder is checked by the key at the index; a global by the shapes of the realm's lexical declarations and of the global object; a closure variable where its cell points; a string's length and its methods from String.prototype. The guard is data in the object: nothing to invalidate, no cache. What a site takes comes from the frame's values when the loop is translated and from learn exits (the interpreter looks at what missed, the site takes it, the loop is translated again, at most 12 times); the shapes the code compares against are marked by the collector through the function. New types in the translation: objects (P), any value (V), entries under the loop's own stack (M, a try's catch offset: such a loop was refused before).
  2. Calls (jit_call_insn, j_inline, j_math, j_char_code_at). A small function of straight-line code that only reads and computes is inlined, the callee guarded; a deopt in it leaves the call to the interpreter as if it had not begun (then the loop is translated again with the callee's numbers taken for doubles, then the call is made). Math.abs, floor, ceil, trunc, sqrt, min, max, imul and s.charCodeAt(i) are computed inline. Other natives are called through a helper the engine exports to the module (wj_jit_call), the operand stack and the objects the loop holds written to the frame first; an exception is a throw exit the interpreter unwinds from.
  3. Measured, not kept: calls of bytecode through the helper. A nested interp_run per call is slower than the interpreter's own call: a call of a small function 84 -> 130 ns, a closure counter 74 -> 102 ns, a method call 185 -> 248 ns. A loop that calls bytecode it does not inline stays interpreted.
  4. Found on the way. A compiled loop of a function sent every back edge of the function's other loops through the full dispatch (hot_back_edge tested the function's count of compiled loops): a for-of beside a compiled loop 37 -> 56 ns an element; the hot loop now leaves only at the back edges of the loops the JIT took (jit_loop_taken, asked out of line, hot_jit_taken: inlined in the hot loop's five back edges, the check made the interpreter 3 % slower on nodes10k with the JIT off, and so did a throw exit of its own in interp_run's back edges, 4 %; a call that threw now leaves the call to the interpreter with jit_rethrow as its callee, which throws the exception pending). Writing whole Value words (the tag's padding and the payload's high word zeroed) in the deopt stubs made a compiled switch loop 1.36 -> 1.62 ns (Cranelift's code for the larger stubs), with no reader of those bytes in the engine: the code writes the bytes the interpreter reads, as before. jitcheck.js ended at tail(1000) (a tail call recurses through the native call path and overflowed the guest's stack in both runs): tail(100), and the 400 lines after it now run.

What neither step changes: what calls bytecode it does not inline (the closure counter, fib, the comparator of sort, which the native calls), allocates (new Point, literals) or concatenates strings; the 4 % of the spread case is its function's code, not compiled either way.

What deopts, and when: a learn exit when a site meets an object of another shape, a value of another type, a string, or a callee that is another function (the loop translated again); a deopt when the shape is one the site does not read inline (an accessor, a proxy, a frozen property written), an int overflows, an index is out of an array, a callee inlined meets what it was not translated for (the call is then made by the interpreter, and the loop translated without inlining it), a held array changed kind after a call; a throw exit when a native called throws. In jitcheck.js (722 lines compared, interpreted against the JIT): 43 loops compiled, 9 refused, 228 deopts.

nodes10k (jspage -image, a timed copy: build() p50 of 400 frames, 3 runs each, interleaved): with the JIT 11.00 (10.99-11.06) -> 11.11 (11.11-11.16) ms, without it 11.01 (11.01-11.06) -> 11.02 (10.91-11.06) ms; its loops call DOM getters and concatenate strings, which the JIT does not take (one is compiled and leaves at its first getter, 16 times).

Tests: jitcheck.js (above), test262 with the JIT 49/82220 errors before and after (0 regressions), interpreted the same; jitcheck.js under a collection every 8 KiB with poisoned cells (-define:JSRT_GC_STRESS=8192 -define:JSRT_GC_POISON=true): the same; judge capi 64 checks.

Not done: whole functions compiled by their call counts (a recursive fib, a function called from interpreted code); calls of bytecode that is not inlined (a direct call into compiled code, which needs the callee compiled whole); the allocation of objects and arrays in compiled code (new Point, {a, b}, [i, j]: such a loop stays interpreted); string concatenation and comparison by value; callees with branches (a ?:); polymorphic inlining.

#What changed, round 21: the JIT compiles functions, calls them directly, makes objects and strings, reads DOM attributes

What round 20 left, in its order (engine/jit.md). Measured with jsengine run -jit -image <engine> on examples/jsbench/micro.js, macro.js and realworld.js, every engine image of the round in turn, 5 rounds (the median, the range in brackets); DOM loops and nodes10k in jspage -image (a timed copy of nodes10k: build()'s p50 over 400 frames). Other agents built and ran test_all on the machine for part of the round: the series below are the ones taken while it was quiet, and a step's figures were checked again on their own where a series was hit.

  1. Whole functions (jit_fn_enter, Jit_Info.fn). A function without loops of its own is compiled once its calls reach javascript.jit.call_threshold (500 now, passed to the engine: the glue had ignored it), as the region [0, end) entered at its call: where frame_push pushes the callee's frame (jit_pushed), in interp_call (jit_entered), in the helper of compiled code. The interpreter's own code is as it was but for frame_push's last line and interp_call: the same hooks in interp_run's call paths and in hot_call made interpreted code 5 % slower with the JIT off (a selection of macro.js, 3 runs: the native calls, class new, destructuring), measured and moved. Measured, not kept: not entering a small function compiled from the interpreter (under 16 bytes of bytecode, whose entry might cost more than its code saves): an interpreted loop calling two such functions 220 ns either way.
  2. Direct calls (j_direct_call). Compiled code calls a function that can be compiled whole (any closure of its bytecode) itself: the callee's frame pushed on the value stack exactly as frame_push pushes it, its code called through the engine's table (imported by the module), the frame popped as frame_pop pops it. No state of the caller lives across the call but in its frame (frames in memory, as today: nothing to save around the call); the callee leaving other than by its return is finished by the interpreter (jit_call_finish). A first version through the helper (frame_push, then the callee's code) was slower than the interpreter (fib 78 -> 104 ns a call): the helper's layers cost more than the call. Compiled code nested on the host stack is bounded (JIT_MAX_NEST): a recursion deeper than that is interpreted, to the same depth limit.
  3. Objects made by compiled code (jit_new, j_prop_add, jit_define_field). Plain objects, literals, arrays and constructions from a helper of the engine (its allocator and collector unchanged: the code reaches a safe point only through a call, which writes what it holds to the frame first); a property appended through the shape's transition (a constructor's this.x = x), a literal's fields with no guard (the shape the code made is known until a join).
  4. Strings (jit_add, jit_streq). + of a string and s += x by the engine's concatenation (ropes, append buffers), done only when no conversion could run code or throw (else the interpreter makes it, once); === of strings by value.
  5. Getters and DOM objects (j_call_getter, Shape.version). Native getters called (as the hot loop calls them: call_native; through call_internal the DOM walk below was 790 ns, not 530), an exception exact through the context's thrower (the interpreter makes the read again and throws); DOM wrappers ordinary objects, the Web IDL prototypes (dictionaries) walked past, guarded by their version. A global's accessor (window.document) is not called: there is no object on the stack to put the thrower in, and a throw exit of the interpreter's back edges was measured 4 % in round 20. nodes10k's building loop reads document and stays interpreted.
  6. Natives called as the hot loop calls them (jit_call): a native function called through call_native directly, without call_internal's dispatch (macro.js's native calls in compiled loops, 5 runs, base, 5, 6: array push/pop 116 (114-125), 117, 107 (105-112) ns; Set add/has 168 (166-259), 169, 150 (149-154) ns; Math.sin / sqrt / pow 160 (155-230), 164, 147 (146-189) ns: from 5 % slower than the base to 8 to 10 % faster).

#What changed, round 22: what the user does while the page's script is busy

A page's script, its events, timers, styles, layout and paint run on the window's thread; only a long layout pass goes to the page thread (page_thread.odin). While a script runs, the Wasm engine's epoch hands the thread to the chrome (shell_preempt), which makes chrome frames between two instructions of the guest (shell_frames.odin): the chrome is built with the input that came, the page area shows the page's last frame (its pixels, kept on the GPU), and input meant for the page waits, in order, for the page's turn. What follows the user then is what a chrome frame can do without the page. Ladybird's text-selection drags off its main thread are the model: the press goes through the page (a listener may cancel it), then the drag follows at once and the page sees the selection when it next gets a turn.

The audit. examples/site/busy.html (a slider for the length of a task, 100 to 400 ms, a loop of them or one; text to select, a link with a :hover style, a field, a scroll box, boxes with CSS animations of transform and opacity, a tall page), and its hold(): one task that keeps the thread until the window's height changes. Measured headless in the e2e harness's process: e2e.while_busy (src/e2e/busy.odin, src/browser/busy_input.odin) gives the chrome frames made under that task one step each (an event, a capture of that frame, the new height that ends the task), so what is checked does not depend on when the script runs; a step is a chrome frame, 12 to 30 ms apart there. "Follows" below: the frame after the input shows it; "waits": nothing moves until the task ends (the rest of it, up to its whole length).

while the page is busybeforeafter
the wheelfollows: the page's last pixels move, what was below the fold is blankfollows, painted from the page's last layout: what comes into view is there
Page Down, Space, the arrows, Home, End (the page has the keyboard)waitsfollows when no keydown / keyup / keypress listener could see the key, no form control has the focus and the document is what the key scrolls; else waits
the thumb of the document's scroll barwaitsfollows (the press, its moves and its release are the shell's, as in a full frame)
a container's scroll barwaitswaits
a text selection's dragwaits (the DOM's selection right once the task ended)follows: the highlight from the last layout; the DOM's selection, selectionchange, the moves the page sees: when the task ends, as before. Not with a mousemove / pointermove listener anywhere, nor before a first selection with a selectstart one
hover (:hover restyle)waitswaits (a restyle is the page's)
the caret's blinkfrozenfrozen (60 captures over 1.8 s: no change)
CSS animations of transform and opacityfrozenfrozen (the same captures)
resizing the windowthe chrome at the new size every frame, the page's last frame anchored at the top leftthe same
switching tabs (a click on the tab strip)follows: the other tab's last framethe same
the menus, the address bar with the mousefollowthe same
Ctrl+L, Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+Page Up / Down with the page's keyboardwait (the keys are the page's first; the commands were queued for after the task)follow when no key listener could see them (the commands that act on the chrome alone run in the chrome frame: the address bar, the next or previous tab)
the release of a press made before the tasklost: it went to the chrome, the page never had its mouseup (a drag left selecting)the page's, after the task, with the drag's moves even outside the page area
  1. A drag's selection under a busy page (selection_shell.odin Sel_Preview). The press is the page's turn's, as before: pointerdown, mousedown and the gesture begin there. A move under a long task waits for the page in deferred as any input; the chrome frame also works out what it will select (gesture_range, the anchor and focus of the gesture's unit from the last layout, selection_preview_move) and paints the page again from its last layout with that range (shell_paint_layout). Nothing of the page changes: the DOM's Selection is the one the task began with (the test reads getSelection() at the task's end: empty), no selectionchange fires under it. When the page has its turn, the moves are given to it in order and each extends the selection as it would have then (extend_to), and the selection's change is one selectionchange (HTML's "schedule a selectionchange event" is a flag: the moves of one turn coalesce). The preview goes then; it stays only where the task changed the document (the layout older than it: Selection_Shell.stale, the gesture extends to the pointer once laid out again, which it did not before: a move made while the layout was stale was dropped). What I chose from the specs: UI Events makes mousemove cancelable but cancelling it does not stop a selection in browsers (Chromium, Firefox); a drag is stopped by mousedown or selectstart being cancelled (Selection API, "selectstart": cancelable, fired before a selection begins). So the preview is shown only when no move can run the page's code: no mousemove or pointermove listener on any node or the Window (page.page_listens), and no selectstart listener before the gesture has started a selection. A listener that the page adds during the task is not seen (the preview is what the eye sees; what the page observes is always its turn's).
  2. Painting a busy page from its last layout (shell_frames.odin shell_layout_paintable, shell_paint_layout). What a page's frame was painted from besides its layout is noted (Paint_Source: the document's mutations, its images' and canvases' pixels, its form controls' serial, its style rules), and while none of it has moved, the layout is not on the page thread, the page has no frames (their documents are laid out when painted) and the window has its size, a chrome frame paints the page again from that layout through the compositor's pictures: the same pixels but where the shell changed something (the scroll, a drag's selection). A script that changed any of it (textContent, a canvas, a field's value) keeps the last pixels, as before: the screen never shows a script's work half done. The wheel used to move the pixels only (blank below them); the document's scroll is now also taken before the input that waited (it was aimed at what the screen showed), not after it.
  3. The scroll bar's thumb (shell_bar_event): a press on the thumb of the document's bar as the last frame drew it (the snapshot's bar, at the scroll shown) starts the tab's Scrollbar_Drag, the moves scroll the document as the wheel does, the release ends it; a drag begun in one kind of frame goes on in the other. Not while presses or keys the page has not had wait (they must not be overtaken), not a container's bar (its offsets are the layout's).
  4. Keys (shell_page_key): with the page's keyboard and no key listener anywhere, a key does what the page's turn would do with it: the browser's shortcuts (browser_shortcut, now one procedure for both) and the tab keys go to the chrome, the modifiers too, and the keys that scroll the document scroll it (keyscroll.odin, its container search and the document's step split out: key_scroll_container, key_scroll_document). Commands that act on the chrome alone are no longer queued for after the task (Command.chrome_only: nav.focus_address, tab.next, tab.previous).
  5. The moves and the release of a press the page had (main.odin route_page_input, shell_route): a press on the page in a full frame is noted (press_to_page, which chrome frames only set for their own presses), so a release under a long task waits for the page instead of going to the chrome (the gesture used to stay down, selecting under a button that was up), and the drag's moves outside the page area wait for it too, as a full frame gives them.

Before and after, on busy.html under hold() (headless, e2e.while_busy): a drag, the thumb, Page Down and Ctrl+L showed in no chrome frame (the first frame that showed them was the one after the task: the rest of the task, 100 to 400 ms on the page's slider); they show in the chrome frame after the input (one frame at the display's rate; 12 to 30 ms between two steps headless). A chrome frame that paints from the layout replays the compositor's pictures (a selection change records the chunks it touches again), as a full frame's paint does.

Tests: src/tools/e2e/busy_page.odin (step "input under a busy page"): a drag's highlight in the frames under the task, the task's empty selection and unchanged selectionchange count, the selection and its selectionchange once it ran, the release under the task the page's (a move after it selects nothing more), and with a mousemove listener no highlight and the same selection; the thumb's and Page Down's scroll under the task (the task's scrollY 0, the busy frame the same pixels as the page once it ran, the bar's presses no mousedown), the address field changed by Ctrl+L under the task. Each fails without its change (checked by building the tests against the shell without it).

Not done: hover, the caret's blink and CSS animations under a long task. The three are the page's: :hover is a restyle; the caret is painted inside the control's picture from a timer of the loop, which a running script does not let fire, and the snapshot has it on or off; animations are sampled by the style pass and their matrices set by the layout's paint-only refresh. Making transform / opacity animations tick without the page needs the compositor to own their timelines (the keyframes resolved to matrices and alphas per frame, the chunks of the animated spaces drawn with them): the next step of this list, as is a container's scroll bar and the wheel over a scroll container (both need the layout's offsets of the container, written only by the page's turn).

#What changed, round 23: document read by compiled code, objects allocated inline, accessors of the script's

What round 21 left, in its order (engine/jit.md). Measured as round 21 did (jsengine run -jit -image <engine>, every image of the round in turn, 5 rounds, the median and the range in brackets; nodes10k in jspage -image, a timed copy: build()'s p50 over 400 frames). Other agents ran test suites on the machine for much of the round: each run waited for the machine to be quiet (under 1.5 cores busy besides it) and ran at a high priority; series taken while it was busy are said so.

  1. A global's accessor (jit_global, j_call_getter). window.document is the global object's own accessor; a read of a global has no object on the stack to put the thrower in. Kept: when the next instruction reads a named property of the value (document.createElement), the thrower goes in the result's place with that property as its accessor, and the throw exit resumes at the next instruction, which throws the exception pending. The interpreter's code is not touched (a throw exit of its own in its back edges was 4 % of nodes10k with the JIT off, round 20). The loop was still refused after that: the callee document.createElement was not known at translation (the value of a getter); a call whose callee the translation cannot tell now leaves through a learn exit once (JIT_AUX_CALLEE, Jit_Site.callee), and a read of an unknown object at a site that learned its shape takes what the prototype holds for its hint. nodes10k build() p50, 7 interleaved runs (the quiet ones): with the JIT 9.1 (8.8-9.1) -> 7.9 (7.65-8.1) ms, without it 9.0 -> 9.1 ms (the same). In macro.js the object literal was 57 -> 66 ns at this step alone (code placement, not explained further), made 28 by step 2.
  2. Objects allocated inline (j_alloc, j_ctor_proto). {} cost 58 ns through the helper, of which the allocation itself is little: the call, shape_root_for's map, the temporary root and its drop. The code now pops a block of the pool's class from the free list (zeroed) or cuts it from the bump chunk, links the cell, counts it, charges the heap and its peak, and writes the object, as cell_new and object_new_shape do; a construction reads the constructor's prototype slot (its shape and the value guarded). The collector's contract is the same: no allocation collects, the object is only in the code's hands until its next call or exit. new Point(i, i) 110 (107-160) -> 51 (50-53) ns, {a, b, c} 56.7 (56.3-59.8) -> 28.4 (27.4-30.0) ns; array literals keep the helper (Array_Data and its values: 83 ns).
  3. The two slowdowns with the JIT off, bisected by engine image (round 21's commits, only src/engine/jsrt and the glue's jit.odin taken from each, 7 runs): a closure made and called in a loop 531 (524-558) ns before round 21, 522 at its first step, 565 from its third (shape_transition factored out of add_property, so the JIT could append properties: a closure's four properties each paid the call), 540 (537-562) with it inlined again (kept; round 21 measured that change as nothing, on a noisier machine). try/catch in a loop was not slower: 68.4 (67.7-71.8) before round 21, 69.3 (68.0-73.1) after, 67.4 with this; the 6 % was noise.
  4. Getters and setters of the script's (j_call_setter, jit_setter, jit_accessor_call). Through the helper, as compiled code calls a function (the getter's frame pushed, its compiled code run): a getter in a loop 151 (151-153) -> 78 (77-80) ns, a class's 168 -> 77 ns, a setter 145 (141-412) -> 81 (80-126) ns, macro.js's getter access 184 -> 92 ns. The accessor's call out of line in the helper made Map's size 37 -> 44 ns; inlined, 36.7. The helpers now set the frame's pc to the instruction after the access, as the hot loop does.
  5. Found after the round: the interrupt in a compiled loop that calls. The compiled code gave the interpreter its safe point every JIT_BUDGET iterations whatever the iterations did; the interpreter polls once its native calls count for a poll (NATIVE_CALL_POLL_WEIGHT). With step 1 a document.write flood is compiled, and 16 384 slow writes ran between two polls: past wasm.max_call_ms the page lost its engine (js_hostile_document_write, intermittent). A loop that calls now also leaves for the safe point once interrupt_counter reaches INTERRUPT_POLL_EVERY (a load and a compare at its back edge: the accessor loops above within 1 ns). js_hostile_compiled_native_flood (a compiled loop of big.join(document.title), each ~0.1 ms) fails without it, passes with it.

#What changed, round 24: what still froze under a busy page

Round 22's list, in the order a user feels it: what moves by itself (animations), the scroll boxes, hover, the caret. All of it is drawn by a chrome frame painting the page from its last layout (round 22's shell_paint_layout, while Paint_Source says nothing it was painted from has moved), with values the shell sets on that layout for the one paint and puts back at once (shell_shown.odin Shown): nothing of the page runs in between, and what its scripts read (getComputedStyle, getAnimations(), scrollTop, the boxes) stays what their turn left. Measured as round 22 did, on busy.html under hold() in the e2e harness's process (e2e.while_busy), with a new step, busy_wait (chrome frames until that long has passed: what moves by the clock moves meanwhile).

while the page is busybeforeafter
CSS animations and transitions of transform and opacityfrozen (two captures 400 ms apart: the slid box at x 181 in both, the faded one's red 26 in both)go on: the box at x 184 then 274 (a slide of 200 px/s), red 26 then 49 (a fade of 0.2 a second); at the page's turn the animation's currentTime is the clock's (3 ms off) and the box goes on from where it was shown
the wheel over a scroll containerthe document scrolled instead (166 px); the container never had itthe container scrolls at once (167 px), painted from the layout; the document stays; scrollTop 0 under the task, the offset and the container's scroll event at the page's turn
the thumb of a container's scroll barwaits (the drag happened at the page's turn: the busy frame differed from the page once it ran in 5464 px)follows: the busy frame is the box as the page then shows it; the bar's presses are not the page's
the caret's blinkfrozen (6 captures over 450 ms at a 200 ms blink: all the same)blinks: 2 or 3 of the 5 later captures differ from the first
hover (:hover restyle)waitswaits (below)
  1. Animations the compositor runs (style.timeline_compositor_values, page.animations_compositor_values). The compositor already applies a transform as a slot of its pictures and an opacity around their replays (round 4): a chrome frame only needs the values. They are taken from the page's timeline without moving it: the run's local time advanced on a copy to the frame's time (the pacer's frame_ms, the clock the page's ticks pin), the keyframes the page resolved for the element (apply_run, transition_value on a copy of its cascaded style), then the box's matrix (layout.box_matrix_of) and its group's alpha. No event fires, no run, overlay or clock changes: at its turn the page's tick reaches the same instant from the same clock, so nothing jumps and getAnimations() reads what it would have. Only elements whose effects animate transform, translate, rotate, scale and opacity alone (Chromium's composited animations), whose box has the transform space or the opacity group in the last layout (an opacity of 1 has no group: that box waits for the page), not in a 3D plane, not animated by a script's Web Animations (their timing is the script's to change). A busy page that animates so now has chrome frames at the display's rate where it had none: under three 1 s tasks with a sliding box, 198 to 204 chrome frames, 164 to 260 ms of them (0.76 to 1.24 ms median each, headless): 5 to 9 % of the thread, what full frames would cost it were it not busy. While a style pass's threads run (its wait lends the thread to chrome frames) the timeline is not read.
  2. Scroll containers (Shell_Frames.boxes, shell_wheel_box, shell_box_bar_press). The wheel over the page looks for the container under the pointer that can move that way (wheel_scroller, the full frame's search, asked of the layout with what the chrome frame shows set on it); the offset it shows is kept per container and painted as the layout's offset (l.scroll, a slot of the pictures). At the page's turn, before the input that waited (as for the document), the layout takes it (set_scroll), and its next frame fires the container's scroll as for any scroll (scroll_events.odin compares offsets). A press on a container's thumb is found on the layout as a full frame finds it (scrollbar_at), and the drag is the shell's Scrollbar_Drag, which a frame of either kind goes on with. When the layout cannot be painted (the script changed what shows), the wheel over a container waits for the page instead of scrolling the document under it.
  3. The caret (forms_shell.odin caret_phase): its phase is the clock's since the field's last change, which the full frames read through a timer of the loop (a running script does not let it fire). A chrome frame reads it too, paints the page from its layout when the caret blinks and asks for a chrome frame at each toggle.
  4. Hover: not done. A :hover change is a restyle of the element entering or leaving the state, of what selectors reach from it (:hover .x, :hover + .x, :has(:hover)), written into the page's styles, which scripts read (getComputedStyle, matches(':hover')); showing it off the page's turn needs a second set of styles for those elements and a refresh of the layout pointing at them, a style match in a chrome frame. And a hover that starts a transition (busy.html's #hoverbox) starts it at the page's turn, not when the chrome frame showed it: the box would jump back to its start. Only a hover whose rules change nothing but transform or opacity with no transition could be shown honestly, at the cost of the style match; Chromium and Firefox restyle hover on their main thread too (a busy page shows no hover in them either).

Tests (src/tools/e2e/busy_page.odin, step "input under a busy page"): a slide and a fade under the task (the box at least 40 px further and the faded box's red at least 10 higher after 400 ms; at the page's turn the animation's time is the clock's within 150 ms and the box no further back); the wheel over the scroll box (the box's pixels moved under the task, scrollTop 0 then, the offset, the document's scrollY 0 and the box's scroll event once it ran, the busy frame the box as it then shows); its thumb (the same, and no mousedown for the page); the caret's blink (6 captures 90 ms apart at a 200 ms blink: one differs from the first). Each fails without its change (the tests built against the shell without it: the values above).

#What changed, round 25: what a first load waited for, found by loading it again and again

Item 10 of the list, as it stood after round 18 (and the list brought up to date: rounds 19 to 24 had not been added to it). The browser: wrentool bench perf, profile builds, the base (4e78b4fa: 0.6.30 and the Inventory's commit) and the round's binary in turn, the order turning, 7 runs of each, median, range in brackets; times in ms from the navigation's start. Conditions: other agents built and ran WPT for most of the round (6.7 of the 16 logical processors busy besides the bench at one reading; p10k's first paint then 72 against 62 ms, ranges overlapping: those series are not below). The table below is the last series, taken when the machine had gone quiet (0.5 processors busy just after it). A sheet's parsing and index were measured alone, outside the browser (a program of wb:css and wb:style over p10k's sheet, 87 KB and 2 000 rules, 41 passes a run, the thread's cycles by QueryThreadCycleTime, 11 interleaved runs, and on the loaded machine 15): the same code gave 11 to 19 ms from one run to the next while the others ran, cycles moved with it, so the figures are the quiet series.

The measure. One load is about 30 samples of the window's thread, and nothing above one sample: why round 18 saw no function stand out. p10k_renav and legacy_renav load a page again and again from itself, for as long as -Seconds says. And timers put for the round around the stages (not kept) gave what the samples could not, for one load of p10k, in ms: the parser's thread 20.2 (html.parse_into 10.1, the walk for <style> and css.parse_stylesheet 7.3, decoding and the rest 2.8); the window's thread compute_styles 13.9 (the engine's rebuild 7.2, half of it compiling declarations; the style threads 3.9; the rest 2.8), the layout 15.6, then a second layout of 1.6.

  1. legacy-html.html's task of 18 to 21 ms: the codecs' probe, under the pool's lock (decoder_thread, src/images/pool.odin). Unidentified since round 18, its samples in waits. With callers (WREN_SLOW_MS=10 WREN_SAMPLE_STACK=1) 18 to 25 of the frame's samples read ZwWaitForAlertByThreadId <- images::submit <- page::entry_start: the page's first image waits for Decoder.mu, which the pool's first thread held while it probed the optional codecs (CoCreateInstance of WIC's HEIF decoder). Round 17 took the wait out of decoder_start; the lock stayed. The first thread to claim the probe (codecs.claimed, an atomic) now runs it holding nothing, and a second thread decodes meanwhile. Test: a_submit_does_not_wait_for_the_codecs_probe (images: the pool's lock is free while a gate holds the probe; fails with the lock around it, checked).
  2. A sheet's selectors held 3.3 KB a rule (css/selectors.odin). Each list of a selector was a dynamic array in the sheet's arena, where the default first capacity of eight stays for good, for each compound and each selector, in pages touched once. The lists start at what selectors use (COMPOUNDS_RESERVE, SIMPLES_RESERVE) and split_commas counts first. p10k's sheet 6 711 -> 2 782 KB (a count, the same in every run), and what reads the rules after it gains too: the rebuild below moved without being touched.
  3. A rule's scratch memory goes with it (parse_outer_rule, css/parser.odin). What a rule gathers while it is read (prelude, values, declarations, lists that start at eight) stayed in the sheet's scratch arena until the end: fresh memory for every rule, faulted in and given back. An arena of its own, emptied after each rule outside any other, reads and writes the same memory. Beside it: names and preprocessing have an ASCII path (a name was appended byte by byte through utf8.encode_rune), an An+B no longer goes through the formatter (fmt was 4 % of p10k's parsing).
  4. The rebuild mapped every node of the document to order its sheets (order_sheets, style/engine.odin): a hash table of every node at each rebuild, on the window thread, for the places of a few owners. Now an array by handle index and a walk that ends at the last owner (usually in the head). The program alone has no document: the rebuild cost 1.5 ms more in the browser than alone before (5.7 against 4.17, two series), 0.1 after (3.3 against 3.16). Beside it: one walk of a declaration's values for viewport and container units, an index key starts with two entries, not eight. Test: sheets_follow_their_owners_in_tree_order (style).
  5. The first read of a layout was laid out twice (js_layout_update, src/browser/js_layout_shell.odin). A page's first pass is forced during run_animation_frames (the Animation phase, which is why the report showed no full pass for it), and the frame's own layout then ran an incremental pass over a document nothing had changed: finish, display list and bands, 0.8 to 1.6 ms. layout_stale said why (printed for the round): the images' generation, 2 against 5 on a page with no image, the tab's being that of its last frame. The forced pass now notes the page's generation. Frames of a first paint with a second pass 1.00 -> 0.00 a load (7 runs of 14 loads, no exception).

  6. The profiler. Each of these found the one above it:

Choosing the thread whose cycles moved most found each just after its burst (the counter moves when a thread leaves the processor) and each sample moved the counter of the thread it stopped, sleeping or not: the sampler now takes every thread that ran over a million cycles in the last second, and shows the threads' names. On sustained work it reads well (nodes10k: 799 of 41 217 running, the page thread 226 of 1 839, place_element, finish...); on bursts of a few ms still nothing, and I do not know why. So the brief's profile of the threads was not obtained, the timers above stand for it, and ETW (wrentool trace, an elevated prompt) is what is left to ask.

#What changed, round 26: heavy pages, from the navigation to the load event

Real pages took 25 to 30 s in wrentool sweep. The browser: development builds (build.bat dev, separate modules: no inlining across packages, so string_eq, pool_get and the bounds checks show in the samples as they do not in a release), with the native library quick. Each load in a fresh process with a throwaway profile, cold HTTP cache and cold bytecode cache, the engine's compiled code warm. Three arms, the order turning: base (3c15c689 and the measure of item 1), the round's binary, and the round's binary with network.max_streams_per_host=6; 5 runs of each, median, range in brackets, ms from the first request. Conditions: public sites over the Internet, one visit at a time, two other agents at work on the machine, the pages' ads and videos changing from one load to the next. What is inside these ranges is not claimed. What depends on neither was measured on generated pages on loopback (7 runs, interleaved). The load of two base runs (cnn.com, css-tricks.com) is 0 in their ranges: the 30 s limit ran out first, so the base's medians there flatter it.

The measure. load_ms of the sweep was not the load: api.navigate, then wait_quiet, which takes browser.remote.quiet_ms (400 ms) at the least and up to 4 s on a page that keeps a timer. example.com's 581 ms is a load of 100 ms; the Wikipedia article's 3.9 s is 0.65 s. The 25 s were real pages all the same, and the wait is now settle_ms. wrentool waterfall (src/tools/wrentool/capture/waterfall.odin) gives a first load request by request: the wait for a slot, name, connection, handshake, server, body, protocol, the time with nothing in flight, first paint, DOMContentLoaded, load, -Idle the time to a quiet network. The page's marks and the phases are in Wren.network.

The waterfall. The network is not what these pages wait for. Name, connection and handshake are 20 to 100 ms a host, in parallel; HTTP/2 and 3 are used; a body is in within 10 to 300 ms of its head. What the requests show is the window thread: a script's body in at 377 ms and seen at 2 790 ms. Its samples during the load, base: the engine's code 47 to 68 % on vimeo.com, npr.org, css-tricks.com, bbc.com, theverge.com and spotify.com, 22 % on cnn.com; style 40 % and more on cnn.com and github.com. Of vimeo.com's engine (the guest profiler): the interpreter's own 27 %, compilation 14 %, the collection 13 %, the rest spread out, nothing that stands alone.

  1. A host that answers over HTTP/2 or 3 has network.max_streams_per_host requests in flight (100) (Host_Slots, src/net/client.odin). Six, the limit of HTTP/1.1 connections, held the streams of one connection too; github.com's 374 requests to one host queued for 470 s in all. And a slot was given back by the window thread, so a busy page starved its own requests. network.max_connections_total 64 -> 256. A host has six until its first answer says what it speaks. Test: e2e net_a_burst_goes_out_at_once_on_a_host_that_multiplexes (twenty requests held 400 ms by the server: on HTTP/2 all leave the queue at once, on HTTP/1.1 the seventh after an answer).
  2. A classic script of another origin runs from what a compile thread made of it (js_run, src/page/js_realm.odin). Muted errors were in the bytecode's key and the compile threads did not know of them: every script of a CDN over 64 KB was compiled off the window thread for nothing, waited for, then compiled on it. That is the 14 % above. Test: e2e jsload_a_large_script_of_another_origin_compiles_once (fails without the fix).
  3. Ready scripts give the loop a turn (scripts_pump, javascript.load.pump_slice_ms, 50). The pump ran every script that was ready in one go: no frame, no network between them, though each is a task of its own in HTML. bbc.com was interactive at 371 ms and painted at 3.4 s. Test: e2e jsload_ready_scripts_give_the_loop_a_turn.
  4. The members of the exact :has() anchors are found by each element's keys (Members_Index, src/style/invalidation.odin). After every full pass, on the window thread, every element was tested against every argument. Test: restyle_dom_has_members_found_by_their_keys (a hundred anchors, 300 elements: at most two tests an element).
  5. Two sets of custom properties that differ are told apart by a digest (Custom_Props.digest). A variable changed high in the tree made each element under it flatten every name into a map, only to learn that they differ: one frame of cnn.com took 5 to 20 s, in default_hasher_string and map_rehash_dynamic. Test: custom_properties_digest (the comparison runs under an allocator that panics).
  6. A full pass keeps the classes of each element as bits of their hashes (class_bits_fill, Match_Ctx.class_bits, css.Simple.hash). Most selectors tried on an element name a class it does not have, and each try read its attribute through. has_class 5 % -> 1.4 % of cnn.com's samples, a full pass there 286 ms in the base, 140 after item 4, 120 after this (three single runs of the profile build). Test: class_bits_of_a_full_pass.

#What changed, round 27: memory, what a long session on many sites keeps

The numbers of wrentool sweep: example.com 190 MB of private bytes, a Wikipedia article 500 MB, cnn.com 2 GB, 4.7 GB (6.4 on another day) after 37 sites in one process. Repeated open and close of one site settled near 300 MB: what was kept was kept per site. Headless, development builds, RTX 4070 SUPER, 16 logical processors, other agents building beside it (a third of the machine at one reading); throwaway profiles; every site visited through wrentool sweep -OneProcess, one visit at a time.

The measure. Wren.stats has memory, the heaps and private pages against what each store says it holds; Wren.memoryReport writes the allocations by kind (a heap's segment, a thread's stack from its TEB, a Wasm memory by its 4 GiB reservation, code); wrentool sweep writes memory_<shard>.tsv after each page, and with -MemoryReports a report before and after Wren.memoryTrim. The check build's .live file names the tracked blocks by place. For what those do not see, a throwaway build hooked NtAllocateVirtualMemory and kept the call stack of each commit: not committed.

Where it was, in MB, one tab, after the 16th site (the Guardian), before and after items 1, 3 to 7 below; then after the 21st site (the Verge) with all of them, a trim just made. Before, the style arenas are in the first line:

beforeafter21st site, final code
private bytes2 4191 3642 928

process heaps729473834
mapped by the kernel for the GPU driver, sheets' arenas, the rest630467454
style arenas6959
compiled code763640
thread stacks101011

Of the heaps after 11 sites (check build, 581 MB in use): 259 MB tracked (HTTP bodies 35, bytecode 22, layout arrays 76, decoded images 27, media 25, web fonts 18), 84 MB of temporary arenas, the rest native (Wasmtime's modules and stores, Lexbor, the decoders, DirectWrite).

example.com, 190 MB: 65 MB of regions no NtAllocateVirtualMemory of the process made: they are the GPU driver's, mapped by the kernel (instance buffers and uploads are what they contain), 30 MB of the driver's own writable image sections, 19 MB the engine's code, 30 MB of heaps once the temporary arenas are small (72 KB per thread of font.l1_words in thread-local storage: 7 MB over the 96 threads, of which 68 are the driver's), 6.5 MB of realm, 7 MB of stacks.

What was wrong, by bytes.

  1. The back/forward cache counted a realm for 8 MB (history.bfcache.page_overhead). A news site's is 136 MB: five such pages were "under" the 512 MB limit, and 21 instances lived after 15 sites. page.memory_held now reads the linear memories of the page and of its frames, nodes count 4 KiB (a page of 10 000 nodes takes 50 MB), the limit is 128 MB. A page kept gives back the style arenas and the layout arrays only its next pass would use.
  2. A layout kept its arrays from one document to the next: fragments, lines, segments, sized by the largest page the tab showed: 300 MB after lemonde.fr, carried to every page after it. Past 1 MiB an array goes at the new document (LAYOUT_KEEP_BYTES); the first pass sizes them from the document anyway.
  3. Compiled modules were counted by their code alone: 14 KB of code took 40 KB of private bytes. The JIT made 12 000 of them in 37 sites, all kept. MODULE_BYTES counts the rest, the limit is 64 MB; what is evicted comes back from the disk cache.
  4. Caches sized for one big page, kept for the session: decoded images 512 -> 128 MB, bytecode 64 -> 32, HTTP bodies 64 -> 32 (the last two are on disk).
  5. The key sets of style invalidation were process-wide, never freed: tens of MB after a few dozen sites, and a table no page could give back. They belong to the engine now.
  6. Temporary arenas: every thread that used one kept 1 MiB, 84 blocks after a few sites. 64 KiB now, 1 MiB for the threads of a frame's passes (host.thread_temp_hot). The page thread's kept the size of the largest page laid out (42 MB): a trim takes it back to its first size.
  7. A trim came only when idle: never with an animation on screen. A closed tab or a kept page gone asks for one within a second, at most every 10 s (memory_trim_soon).

The result. wrentool sweep -OneProcess on the same 37 sites, private MB after each, one run of each (one tab; the session ends on apple.com):
