#What changed, round 42: the document's load as two state machines

The pump and the document's life cycle were a bool, a handle, a bool and a float, then four bools beside ready_state. They are Pump_State and Doc_Phase now, with one transition proc each (pump_to, doc_phase_set). A paint turn was a timer of 24 ms; it ends with first_paint_done, or at javascript.load.paint_deadline_ms (100). Development builds, wrentool waterfall, a base binary kept apart, each pair of loads back to back, a load started only with the machine under 25 % busy.

What was found.

  • The frame is not late on these pages: it is long. A trace of the turns: the yield comes, the frame starts in the same few ms, and the turn ends 35 to 270 ms later, inside it. No top-level page of the four reached the deadline. The 100 ms is a bound, not a measured figure.
  • Stripe's hidden frames spent the wait on nothing: a document that is never shown waited for the whole deadline inside npr.org's and cnn.com's load. A frame's document, a page not shown and a page that has missed one deadline get no turn now.

  • The first form of this work was worse on npr.org: first paints of 1.0 to 1.6 s in 3 runs of 11, against none over 811 ms for the base. Two things were changed, and neither alone was shown to be the cause (with the first alone, 1.1 and 1.4 s in 10 runs on a busy machine).

    • A frame held by a sheet ended the turn: one traced run had the reveal attach a body <link> and the frame find the page blocked. The turn now goes on; only a frame that laid the page out and found nothing to show ends it.
    • The reveal went back to the pump before each script, which let what was ready of the async scripts in between the parser's, in front of the body. It stops where it did now, and paint_turn_due is asked by the reveal and by pump_turn.
  • Deferred scripts, modules and async scripts once parsing was done had no turn: the_end never asked, and the others' test read a parser position that parser_finish had reset. They have one now, with the first frame given a chance to run first.

Tests. jsload_a_paint_turn_waits_for_a_late_frame, jsload_a_paint_turn_ends_at_its_deadline_once, jsload_a_deferred_script_goes_behind_the_first_paint, jsload_a_frame_a_script_reached_is_not_loading. The first three on a virtual clock or on no clock at all.

Left. the_end does not wait for sheets before a deferred script, as HTML says it should ("a style sheet that is blocking scripts"): the order of scripts stayed as it was. Doc_Parser.active is .Parsing by another name but for the steps of parser_finish before the phase changes.

#What changed, round 43: functions that never run

Round 34's figures: compile plus bytecode read on the window thread 177 to 430 ms, verify_function 2.7 % of the engine's samples, lazy compilation not built. Measured again on the window thread, from the start to the load event, base (59857708): the front end 4 to 24 ms a load, what was left after round 39 sent scripts of 4 KB and more off the thread; Deserialize 86 to 207 ms; collections 150 to 640 ms, which are not this round's. Heavy pages ship megabytes of bytecode and run little of it. Of gpt.js and a 545 KB prebid bundle in jsengine mem: 5 021 functions, 81 bodies read (they stop at the first DOM call they miss: a page runs more, not measured).

1. Verification at the first run. A flag tested at each entry was weighed: there are at least six ways into a function (frame_push, interp_call, generators, modules, the JIT's entries), and one could be forgotten. A function that has not run has LAZY_CODE as its code instead: one instruction, lazy_body, past OPCODE_COUNT so that no stream can hold it, which leaves the hot loop by its default case, verifies, and starts the frame again. Whatever enters a function ends there, and a call pays nothing: jsengine cost does not move. What a frame needs is in the function's counts; stack_size is checked against the code before the stack is used. At first run, not at the first closure: most functions of a bundle get a closure when their module's scope runs, and never a call. The verifier's temporary tables left the scratch memory, which lasts until the outermost call returns. Verification was not 2.7 %: it was 30 to 45 % of Deserialize.

2. Read at the first run. BC_VERSION 29, QuickJS's 28 but for a function's record: a head (flags, name, counts, position, closure variables without their names), then a body, its length first, with what the head does not have. read_object keeps the stream (Bytecode_Store, counted by the functions read from it), notes where each atom is, and reads the top-level function. A head is read with its parent's constant pool, a body at the function's first run, an atom at its first use: a body nobody reaches is a pos +=, the functions inside it with it. The code is copied out to have its atoms rewritten, so the stream stays as it came: JS_WriteObject hands it out and Function_Bytecode.image, keep_image and one copy go. The line tables and the source are slices of it. The three builtin/*.bin have no source here: they were laid out again by a throwaway converter. The stream is no longer byte for byte QuickJS's: e1j diff-batch against the retired C oracle would now differ in every function.

A failure moves with the read. The top-level function still fails in read_object, so a bad cache entry still means compiling the source. A nested function's failure is a SyntaxError at each of its calls, and that one has no fallback; a cached stream is authenticated, so it takes a bug of ours or a bad disk.

3. Lazy compilation: not built. The bound on the window thread is the front end's 4 to 24 ms, under 0.5 % of a load. The rest of compiling is on the compile threads, and there it would not come out free: early errors want every byte parsed anyway, and of a compile the parse is 60 %, the passes 31 %, the stream 9 % (prebid 30.9, 16.1, 4.8 ms; gpt.js 5.6, 3.6, 0.8; native, median of 9). What it could save is the 40 % of the compile threads' work, and to do so it would compile each function that runs at its first call: on the window thread, the one that is 90 % busy. Parse time moved to the bottleneck, to save time that is not on it.

Read plainly. Deserialize: -44 to -64 %, 41 to 132 ms of the window thread a load, ranges apart on all eight rows. Step 2 alone: ranges apart on cnn.com and npr.org, meeting on the two others; 13 to 46 ms. theverge.com's DOMContentLoaded: -10 and -12 %, ranges apart. Every other DOMContentLoaded, every load, paint and CPU: ranges overlap, so not proven. Six loads of eight went down by the median, but what was saved is 2 to 3 % of a load and the medians move more than that: the window thread's JavaScript stays what it was. Two went up: npr.org warm +5 %, and bbc.com/news warm, from 562 to 1 366 by the median, its CPU with it: that page has three modes, about 500, 1 350 and 2 200 ms (two were seen in rounds 31 to 36), and each series lands elsewhere (2 198 and 2 125 in the first, 2 074 and 1 358 in the second). Ranges overlap; not explained, to be read neither as a gain nor as a loss.

Steady state. jsengine cost: every case within 2 % of the base, 18 of 20 the same to the instruction, because the interpreter's hot path did not change. micro.js, interpreted, 7 runs interleaved, twice: calls better (a small function 67.1 -> 62.0 ns, a method 108 -> 104), simple loops a little worse (nested loops 27.7 -> 28.9, a property set 19.1 -> 20.4, switch 49.9 -> 52.0), most ranges overlapping, the same in the two series. With the same instructions the reading is the code's placement, as in round 36: the image of step 1, with the same hot loop, has these loops at the base's times and instead try/catch +7 % and string concat +4 %, which the round does not have. Likely, not proven. Nothing here was measured with the JIT beside jitcheck's results.

Memory. jsengine mem, the two scripts above, the JS heap after a collection: 7 757 -> 4 481 KiB where the source was compiled, which kept the image before too; about 5 345 -> 4 481 where bytecode is read from the cache (the same less the base's image; not measured on that path). Function cells 5 021 -> 929, atoms 8 749 -> 3 455, tables of code, pools and locals 1 038 -> 74 KB; most of what is left is the stream, 2.4 MB. A page's private bytes do not show it beyond noise: -9 to +3 % by the median over the eight rows, ranges overlapping on all: a realm's heap is little of a process of a gigabyte.

Left, and why.

  • Function sources are 64 and 52 % of those two streams: 2 065 KB for 545 KB of script, 747 KB without them, because a nested function repeats text its parent has. An offset into the outermost function's text would divide the stream, on the disk too, and the memory it keeps. It is its own change of format; measured here only by size.
  • What Deserialize still is: the bodies that run, and their heads, atoms and strings. A run's functions are not known before it; a list of the functions a script ran, kept with its bytecode, could read them off the thread: not measured.
  • Bytecode shared across realms: not touched. Collections are now the largest item of this list: 150 to 640 ms a load.

How a lazily read function is covered. Two lifetimes are new. A body read in the middle of a run makes strings and heads held by nothing yet: rt.gc_disabled for the read, as read_object. A function outlives the top-level function that had the stream: the store counts every function, with no marking to forget; function_bc_finalize releases it, and lazy collects between a script's end and its functions' first runs. All of it under JSRT_GC_STRESS=8192 with JSRT_GC_POISON: lazy interpreted and with the JIT at threshold 1, hotcheck.js, jitcheck.js interpreted and compiled, objectspread.js. The JIT reads the body at its entry when its threshold is 1 and neither compiles nor calls directly what has not run (jit_fn_compilable). judge fuzz went over only what was read, so it now reads every body (bytecode_read_all): 20 000 mutants, then 1 500 of those run, no crash.

Tests. jsengine lazy: a script of 1 000 functions, 10 nested in one of them: reads 1 002 heads and 2 bodies; a second call of a function reads nothing; a first call reads one body; the nested ones come with their parent's body, once; toString reads one; length and name none: exact counts, which an eager reader fails from the first step. In the step of test262 with the JIT, interpreted and at threshold 1. judge capi: a stream with a broken function, its first opcode replaced by lazy_body: it loads, the others run, the call throws SyntaxError, twice. build\test_all.exe -Quick -NoAsan: one step fails, the documentation site, which this branch does not regenerate; test262 with and without the JIT, jitcheck, hotcheck and jsengine cost among those that pass.

Not verified. The release build, a long session, the full WPT, the full test262, AddressSanitizer, Tracy, ETW: not run. Other agents were at work on the machine for part of the series. How much of a real page's functions run: not counted.

#What changed, round 44: what collections cost a load

Round 43 left collections as the largest item of the window thread beyond executing scripts, 150 to 640 ms a load; round 34 said "generations: not started". Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1 in a loop, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load, base (387e8ace) kept apart, the order turning; Gc spans of the thread of the load event, up to it. A build with temporary spans for each stage of a collection, and a census of what each one found, says what follows; it is not in the tree.

What a collection was. One heap per realm: a page, each frame, each worker. Two triggers: the heap past a threshold, at the next safe point, and the DOM's (js_after_task, the document's nodes doubled past 4 096): one or two a load. The first threshold is javascript.gc_threshold_bytes (2 MB), then max(2 x what the last one left, that + 4 MB). A load is 9 (cnn.com) to 19 (npr.org) collections on the page's realm, more on its frames'; those of a heap under 20 MB cost 1 to 3 ms, the last ones of theverge.com 77 to 139 ms each: the cost is in the five largest. They do not find a heap that only grows: 1 252 830 cells become 362 008, 175 MB become 79.

one load, basecollectionsmsmarksweepns a cell sweptns a live cell marked
cnn.com10188601093545
npr.org214801492583055
theverge.com216312013715670
bbc.com/news13200681204457

(All realms and past the load event, the census adding a little to the sweep.) The sweep is 55 to 60 % of a collection, the marking 30 %. The prologue, the roots and the finalizers are the rest, a few ms, but on npr.org while 26 000 wrappers are alive (roots 14, prologue 4, finalizers 6 ms). Of theverge.com's largest heap, what lives: 213 000 objects (124 000 plain, 45 000 arrays, 29 000 functions), 86 000 strings, 36 000 closure cells, 18 000 functions' bytecode: 32 MB of cells in a heap of 79, the rest slots, array storage and script streams, which cost the collector nothing. What dies: 620 000 objects, 176 000 strings, 92 000 closure cells. Plain objects and strings: neither wrappers (a few thousand), nor shapes, nor bytecode dominate.

1. The cells in an array (Runtime.cells, Cell.gc_next gone). Walking the list alone took 40 ns a cell, 53 ms for 1.35 million: each cell's address was in the one before, one cache miss after another. From an array the addresses are known ahead, the misses overlap: 30 to 56 -> 21 to 42 ns a cell. A cell is 4 bytes smaller (Object 56 -> 52, a string 40 -> 36), which an array entry costs back; a realm starts 128 KB larger (6 720 -> 6 848 KiB of linear memory: the list has its capacity at once). The code the JIT writes pushes on the list and leaves for its helper when it is full (j_cell_room). Order kept: newest first, finalizers read what is older. +9 instructions a cell in jsengine cost. On a heap allocated in order and never reused (a temporary bench: 800 000 cells) list and array cost the same: the gain is that of a heap that has been swept.

2. Heap growth at 250 % (javascript.gc_heap_growth_percent, was 200). Dead cells are paid for once whatever the policy, the live ones at each collection: fewer collections cut the marking and the sweep of what lives. 7 runs, median (range), items 1 and 2 only, ms and MB:

collections to the load, 200 %250 %300 %Gc ms 200 %250 %300 %private MB 200 %250 %300 %
cnn.com976131 (105-170)86 (81-104)79 (73-89)9961 0221 021
npr.org191411268 (265-279)200 (187-220)175 (172-280)862901985
theverge.com171310389 (312-514)289 (276-436)209 (205-440)9729971 034
bbc.com/news1198109 (0-138)96 (0-117)79 (9-88)678667700

300 % takes 25 to 80 ms more off and costs 40 to 80 MB more on the two largest: the line is 250. A growth by the load's phase or by the survivors was not built: half the heap dies at the large collections of these loads, so the survivors would not have told it to wait.

3. The sweep by steps (Gc_Sweep, gc_sweep_step). After the marking nothing reaches a dead cell: weak references cleared, caches pruned, host finalizers run; a dead cell only waits. Past 65 536 cells the sweep stops being one pause: the threshold is put 128 KB above the heap, and each time the safe point finds it passed, 8 192 cells are swept per 128 KB allocated since the last step (compiled code polls seldom: a step can be large). The mutator's new cells go after those of the marking. What the collection left is the heap less what was allocated since, so the next threshold does not grow with the sweep's length. gc_collect (the host's, js.collect) still does all at once; so do a census, the teardown and a memory limit reached (gc_sweep_finish). The total does not change; the longest pause is the marking.

Of the 200 ms that leave the thread on theverge.com not all come back: a heap that grows further is memory touched for the first time, and cold. bbc.com/news has its modes (a load of 500 to 900 ms, or of 2 s): its medians say which mode came up more often, and nothing of this round; its pause and Gc are read within the 2 s mode.

Private: 0 to +7 % (+57 MB at worst). Realm memory: +10 to +24 %, 24 to 106 MB: a linear memory never shrinks, so a heap's peak stays as its size, and a peak is now 2.5 x what is live where it was 2 x. Item 2 is the cause: item 1 alone is within 3 % of the base in private bytes, either way, and item 3 within 2 % of item 2. Why the private bytes move less than the linear memories was not looked into.

Steady state. jsengine cost: every case within 2.5 % of the base, new Promise 7 % less. micro.js, interpreted, 7 runs interleaved, median per test: new Point 209 -> 190 ns, geometric mean of the 21 tests 0.98.

Measured, not kept.

  • Reading ahead in the sweep (a load of the cell 12 entries on, Wasm having no prefetch): sweep against marking the same on all four pages, one load each.
  • A ring in the marking (a cell's mark read 8 cells after its address is met, so its miss overlaps; what OCaml 5 does): 44 -> 42 ms on a bench of 800 000 live cells: not worth a subtle marking (a value in the ring is not marked yet when the weak pass asks).

Left, and why.

  • Generations: not built. A nursery needs a write barrier in the interpreter's stores, the natives' and the JIT's, or moving cells, which nothing here can do (host handles, addresses in bytecode and in compiled code). What it would remove is what is left: of theverge.com's 833 000 objects at its largest collection 620 000 were dead, and would never be touched. The simpler means got 40 % at no risk to the stores; the barrier is a round of its own, on the JIT's and the hot loop's instruction count.
  • The marking is now the pause: 37 ms on theverge.com, of which the roots and the wrappers' prologue 3 to 8; 24 on npr.org. Incremental marking needs the same barrier.
  • The DOM's trigger stays: it is 1 or 2 collections a load, and the removed nodes wait for it.
  • javascript.gc_threshold_bytes said the wrong thing ("half the live heap"); it says what it does now. Its floor (JS_SetGCThresholdFloor) is stored and read by nothing: the first threshold is all it sets.

How the new states are covered. A cell's list and its survivors: jsengine gc, interpreted and compiled (the code's own allocation past the list's first growths): 20 000 objects kept are 20 000 cells more after a collection, to the slack of a script's own; all still readable after a million of garbage, cells back where they were. Collections per volume: as many as the garbage over 1.5 x the heap, within a quarter (18 interpreted, 15 compiled; about 27 at 200 %, past the margin). Steps: more steps than sweeps, when interpreted. Under JSRT_GC_STRESS=8192 with JSRT_GC_POISON, the lazy path on from the first cell, a step of 4 096 cells each 2 KB: hotcheck.js, jitcheck.js (interpreted, compiled), objectspread.js, recursion.js, jsengine lazy (both): pass; jsengine gc passes but for its count of collections, which stress changes on purpose. A finalizer runs in creation order, newest first, whether between two steps or not, so a function still finds its bytecode and an iterator its map; a block freed by a step can be reused by the mutator, which is the one thing new, and no finalizer reads what is newer than its cell.

jsengine cost now collects before it measures: where a collection fell moved a case by up to 550 instructions an iteration when a heap's size changed by a byte, which is not the path it says it measures. wrentool waterfall has one column more, what the pages hold.

Tests. build\test_all.exe -Quick -NoAsan: test262 with and without the JIT, the leak checks of web_jsdom, memory_growth: pass. a font on its way holds its text failed once with 12 steps at work, a first paint before the font, and passed alone: a matter of time in that test, not of this round, not investigated further.

Not verified. The release build, a long session, the full WPT, the full test262, AddressSanitizer, Tracy, ETW: not run. The slow runs of the machine came in these series too. A sweep that is interrupted by a memory limit: read, not tested by a count.

#What changed, round 45: what is left of a load is the speed of the scripts

No code changed in this round: it asks what a load is still waiting for, on the tree with text decoration merged.

No regression from the merge. Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1, 4 runs interleaved against 5cbd26be: theverge.com load 4 213-4 305 before, 4 247-5 169 after, CPU 7 156-8 656 and 7 406-8 766; cnn.com load 3 887-4 197 and 3 614-4 178, CPU 6 125-6 812 and 6 281-6 609; first paint the same. A single run of 6.7 s came out of nothing but the machine: one run proves nothing here.

The page thread does not wait. One load of theverge.com under WREN_SPANS, by 500 ms: wait 86 ms in the first bucket and none after, Guest 200 to 900 ms in nearly every bucket, about 4.7 s of a 7 s trace; Gc 302, Deserialize 124, Compile 21, Jit 7. Compile_Wait adds up to 939 ms but it is no block: it runs from a script's arrival to its bytecode being taken. recaptcha__en.js is compiled in 222 ms and taken 840 ms later, because the thread is running other scripts, in order. Taking bytecode sooner would change nothing.

So the rest is execution. javascript.jit.call_threshold was measured in round 39: 10 000 costs CPU and 1 000 doubles it, Cranelift costing more than the code it makes gives back. Not run again.

Left. A baseline compiler was the idea: code made cheaply would let a low threshold pay. The nearest measure says otherwise. wasm.wasmtime.opt_level=none keeps the shipped engine and compiles only what the JIT makes without optimising, 3 runs: theverge.com CPU 8.5-9.0 s at speed and 100 000, 8.5-10.7 at none, 9.8-11.8 at none and 10 000, 17.5-19.8 at none and 1 000; load 5.2-5.3, 5.0-6.4, 5.1-6.2, 5.5-7.2 s. npr.org load 3.8-4.4 at speed, 4.5-5.9 at none, 5.0-5.2 at none and 1 000. What compiling early costs is not only Cranelift's optimisation. The single-pass register allocator for the whole engine is worse still, 3 runs: theverge.com load 4.0-4.3 s becomes 7.2-7.5, npr.org 3.8-3.9 becomes 6.4-9.6 (whether the shipped code was still used was not checked). Not tried: a compiler written for this, which is why this is no proof. Winch is out: it takes the whole engine with it (theverge.com 6.1 s against 4.4, one run) and its code does not mix with Cranelift's. Generations in the collector can take at most what Gc is, 300 ms here.

#What changed, round 46: what the interpreter and the runtime spend on a page

Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1 in a loop, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load, base (90c6e06c) kept apart, the order turning; Guest: the outermost calls into the engine on the window thread, up to the load event (WREN_SPANS). Public sites; a second agent was at work on the machine for part of the series.

The measure. WREN_WASM_PROFILE and WREN_JS_PROFILE each take their samples where the code polls, and both misled this round (below). A temporary change of WREN_SAMPLE_STACK, not in the tree, wrote the whole walked stack of each 1 ms sample of the window thread with the allocation of its instruction pointer; a throwaway script named the frames from the ELF of build/js/wren_js.code (the engine's allocation holds that file, so an address less its base is an offset in it) and from the linker's map. No poll in it: a sample of the engine says the instruction, and objdump -D -b binary -mi386:x86-64 on the bytes of a function says which. One load each, the share of Guest, a frame's sample going to the innermost category on its stack, %:

The profile is flat, and almost nothing of a load runs in the code the JIT makes: 2 samples of 2 266 on theverge.com. What stands out is what is not the interpreter: an algorithm, twice.

1. A greedy loop of one character, in the matcher (lre_exec.odin). d of concert_ads.js, 6 % of theverge.com's script, is /\S+(@|%40)\S+\.\S+/.test(url). As bytecode a run is a state pushed and an instruction dispatched for each character, then again going back; and it is quadratic: the search starts again at each position of the token. exec_backtrack now recognises x+ and x* of one character (\S, a class, .) as the compiler emits them, the format unchanged, and takes the run at once, with one state of a new kind for all its positions (.run: the state and an undo record of the low end), going back only to where the character that follows the loop can match. exec_search: a regexp that starts with a run, without back references, goes on after the run when it fails, since what follows was tried at each position a later start could reach. That pattern on a URL of 150 characters, native, 2 000 tests: 442 -> 8 ms (Node 40). Regular expressions of theverge.com 6.1 -> 2.2 % of Guest. \w+ and [^"]* on short subjects: 55 -> 53, 174 -> 158 ms, what is left there is the call.

2. indexOf a word at a time (units_index_of). OtAutoBlock.js looks each script up in a table of thousands of tags (d.indexOf(F), k.Tag.indexOf(d)): str_index_of was 9 % of npr.org's Guest. The first and last units of the pattern are tried on 8 bytes (or 4 wide units) at once with the zero-byte trick; ctz gives the first candidate. 1 MB: 24 -> 10 ms, short strings 106 -> 91 (the call is most of those). sp_index_of 9 -> 3 % of npr.org.

3. Names nothing has (Name_Filter, js_dom_collections.odin). window.x, typeof x of a name no script defined reach the window's named properties, and each was getElementsByName: a walk of the document. It now filters before it makes objects, and neither compiles nor sorts what is empty. 3 000 calls among 300 marks, a page of its own, 5 runs: 2 914 (2 906-2 955) -> 144 (142-146) ms. On theverge.com it does not show: 2.1 -> 1.9 % of Guest, what is left being the JSON below.

#What changed, round 47: four engineering ideas measured before they were built

No code of the engine changed in this round but for tests: hotcheck.js holds the matcher's runs, and the codec probe test no longer takes the moment the pool's other thread holds the lock for the probe's. The matcher of round 46 was compared with Node on 41 500 random regexps over random subjects: 11 differences, all /u where V8 stops in the middle of a pair and Wren goes by AdvanceStringIndex. test262's built-ins/RegExp: 0 errors in 1 879 tests.

Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1, interleaved, ms; Guest: the window thread's outermost calls into the engine, whole trace (so past the load event). Public sites, each change a temporary one, none in the tree.

Scripts of frames on their own threads: no. Guest by realm, one load. The frames' realms on the window thread hold 148 of 2 158 ms on cnn.com (7 %), 119 of 4 810 on npr.org (2.5 %), 38 of 3 897 on theverge.com (1 %). That is all such threads could take off, before what crossing them costs. theverge.com's 732 ms of another realm are a worker, already on a thread of its own.

Inline caches: no. The interpreter has none (hot_find searches at each get_field). The ceiling was measured rather than the thing built: a direct-mapped cache of (shape, atom) to holder and slot, 4 096 entries, without the guards of the prototype chain a real one needs, 5 runs:

load baseload cacheGuest baseGuest cache

npr.org3 602-3 9913 562-3 9173 973-4 4274 035-4 183
theverge.com3 686-3 7773 782-3 854 (2 runs)3 623-3 8573 585-3 642 (2 runs)

theverge.com's 3 other runs ended at about 700 ms with the page's scripts broken: without guards the cache gives wrong answers, and those runs say nothing. No load gained; guards would take some of what is left. As round 46 read it, the time of a lookup is the misses on the object and the shape, which a cache does not avoid.

JIT profiles kept across visits: no. What they would give is compiled code early. javascript.jit.call_threshold 2 000 against 100 000, 4 runs: ten times as many translations on the window thread (Jit 122 ms in 1 225 spans against 10 in 90 on theverge.com), Guest 3 728-3 837 against 3 577-3 868 and 4 157-4 416 against 4 045-4 285 on npr.org, theverge.com's load 4 176-4 284 against 3 705-3 807. Not the same thing as code there from the first call, which was not measured; but the code that came earlier took nothing off, and attaching it stays on the window thread however it was made.

Generations in the collector: no measured gain in a load. gc_collect turned off, 4 runs: theverge.com Guest 3 575-3 698 -> 3 352-3 470 (-6 %), its load 3 696-3 873 -> 3 675-3 913; cnn.com and npr.org nothing, inside their ranges. This is not the whole of the collector: Gc spans remained (theverge.com 450-510 -> 280-320 ms, about as many spans) and what still makes them was not traced. javascript.gc_threshold_bytes at 1 GB is no measure of it, it only moves the first collection.

Threaded dispatch by tail calls: not built, by arithmetic. hot_loop and interp_run are 10 to 41 % of Guest (round 46) and 22 % of hot_loop's samples are at the dispatch: 2 to 9 % of Guest is the whole of what it could touch, for a rewrite of every instruction, the JIT's exits included. Not measured.

Read plainly. A Guest 6 % shorter on theverge.com did not move its load, in two of these series. What ends these loads is no longer the sum of the script's time; what does was not established here. In order: what scripts force of style and layout (43 % of cnn.com's Guest), then the critical path to the load event itself.

#What changed, round 48: what ends a load, and what a forced read pays for

Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1 under WREN_SPANS, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load, base (269c7ae2) kept apart, arms interleaved, the order turning. Temporary code, none in the tree: what the_end waited for at each look, laps inside page.styles and restyle_dom, what marks_keyed_scan marked and through which anchor. Public sites.

What a load waits for last. Each line: what the_end waited for last, two loads a site, then the script's life as the spans give it.

the last wait
cnn.comboltPlayer, 3.4 MB, in order, then boltInstancerequest +2 684, last byte +3 037, off-thread compile 414 ms, run +3 464, load +3 587
npr.orgjwplayer's player.js, 1.2 MB, async; in one run of two two posters and a frame of Stripe after itrequest +2 847, seen +3 398, compile 164 ms, run +3 566, load +3 617
theverge.coma chain of async scripts: gtm.js, bounce's runtime, main-v2, ads-v2, jQuery, then recaptcha's framefive hops, each a script that inserts the next

The network is not on the path. The last byte of a request comes 10 to 100 ms after it starts. What is long is the time until the page hears of it: theverge.com's main-v2 had its last byte at +54 ms and reached the page at +814, behind a task of 738 ms (wj_run_jobs). The window thread is busy for 85 to 95 % of the time up to the load event: 3 606 of 3 817 ms on theverge.com, 3 241 of 3 618 on npr.org, 3 062 of 3 588 on cnn.com, and an idle frame of cnn.com's still takes 6 of its 16 ms. npr.org's three longest tasks, 812, 563 and 519 ms, are JavaScript from end to end.

A wait that no span called one. Of 738 ms of cnn.com's inline Script, the first 316 are no Guest: the window thread stood in compile_ahead_wait, the 3 MB inline script's compile not done at its turn (a futex: 14.8 % of the samples of frames over 30 ms, under js_run). Everything queued behind it, among others launch-*.min.js, an async script compiled at +581 ms that ran at +1 439: it is what asks for vendor, app and through them boltPlayer.

1. A long inline compile holds the parser, not the thread (compile_ahead_holds). An inline script of 256 KB and more whose compile is under way goes to Doc_Parser.pending, as one that waits for a sheet does; compile_done takes the pump up again. Async scripts, arrivals, timers and frames go on. On cnn.com the head of that chain runs at +677 instead of +1 439, vendorHashes is asked for at +875 and not at +1 959, and boltPlayer's compile no longer ends with the window thread idle: it now overlaps the page's own work. jsload_a_long_inline_compile_holds_the_parser_and_not_the_loop, with the compile threads held by the test (compile_hold).

What a forced read costs. Reads before the load event, one load, Host spans of 20 us and more:

A few reads each pay the catch-up of what the scripts changed since the last one: a call of getPropertyValue that takes 95 ms is a style pass, the string costs nothing. 2. A container's size that flips nothing restyles nothing (cq_size_settled). restyle_containers restyled the whole subtree of each container whose size moved, on one thread: 60 ms on cnn.com and npr.org for a container high in the page, 12 to 17 ms a time on theverge.com, and most of them for the first size a container gets. It now asks the conditions of the page's @container rules (Engine.container_conds) at the old size and the new: a rule holds on True alone, so a first size from Unknown to False flips nothing. No flip and no cq unit in force (Engine.container_units, in a sheet or a style attribute: compile_declarations sees both): the container's context takes the size in place, for what is restyled later. style() beside a size feature: any feature that moves counts. All style before the load event, the sum of the table: theverge.com 355 -> 284 ms, npr.org 444 -> 402, cnn.com 967 -> 931, whose cqw and cqi keep the walk. The conditions live with their sheets: one that leaves without a rebuild ends this until the next (Engine.container_conds_lost), as does a sheet of a shadow tree with such rules. container_size_that_flips_nothing_restyles_nothing, container_not_of_an_unknown_size, container_units_restyle_at_any_size, container_conditions_go_with_their_sheet.

Measured, built, not kept.

  • A body held back at its first MB. network.queue.high_water_bytes, 1 MiB by request, stops the reading of a body while the window thread does not take it: cnn.com's 3.4 MB took 310 ms and npr.org's 1.2 MB 394 ms in a load, 33 to 70 and 23 to 46 ms by themselves (node, the same files, HTTP/2 with a large window). An exemption for bodies kept whole, then the network stack's thread handing a script's body straight to a compile thread (the compile of player.js ended 330 ms before the page's turn came). It worked, measured by the spans, and took nothing off a load: without either, 7 runs: cnn.com 2 607 against 2 748, theverge.com 3 608 against 3 582, npr.org 3 466 against 3 603, ranges overlapping; CPU +5 to +9 %, npr.org's Guest to the load 2 509 -> 2 730: what came sooner was work that used to follow the load event. With a thread 90 % busy, a script that is ready sooner waits for its turn instead.
  • A document's long inline scripts found in its bytes by the same thread, compiled before the parser is done: 9 runs, cnn.com 2 689 against 2 624, DOMContentLoaded 1 581 and 1 581.
  • :has(+ .x) read by the place of a change. An element that comes or goes changes a pair of siblings only if it, or the one after it, carries a key of the argument; + reaches as many elements before it as it has steps. Correct against a full pass, and on cnn.com it took 27 ms off 501: most of the elements restyled come from anchors whose answer really flipped (a member left), the subject keys of :has(...) .x restyled with no change to show. Taken out.

Hypotheses retracted.

  • "The network path halves cnn.com's tail": the first series gave it 14 %, and it was the hold, built with it. The arm without it showed that.
  • _extendhfsf2 (4.5 % of page::styles) and strncpy, handle_error in the compiler's profile are no half floats, no string copies and no bounds failures: nothing calls them there. The names are the nearest symbols of code with none of its own.
  • WREN_RESTYLE_TRACE makes passes dearer than they are: read for times it said 1 187 ms of style on cnn.com where the sampler and the laps say 500 to 900. It names passes; it does not time them.

Left, by what was seen. An element restyled costs 50 to 90 us on the window thread, and on cnn.com nine in ten change nothing: 11 000 elements, 470 ms. Matching is flat (matches_simple 15 %, matches_compound 6, :has() 12 %); an ancestor compound such as body:not(...) is looked for by walking up (parent_element 5 %). watch_prepare after each full pass: 14 to 23 ms of cnn.com's 80, six times a load. Full passes: a sheet came with @keyframes that elements use 40 to 85 ms a page, once. Layout: 25 full passes of 5 to 10 ms on theverge.com, too much changed: a positioned child of <body> has no plan (simple_child_style), so its container is rebuilt. The container walk of pages with cq units (cnn.com). getComputedStyle still lays out; on these pages a layout is a tenth of a read. The compiler: 414 ms in Wasm for boltPlayer, 230 to 260 natively (judge speed, 14.7 MB/s; judge prof now samples without deadlocking on the heap), flat; since the hold it is no longer the last wait of cnn.com.

Not established. Why a Guest 6 % shorter (round 47) left theverge.com's load where it was. What is known: its load event waits for a chain whose steps queue behind whatever the window thread has, and npr.org above shows the same load with 8 % more Guest before it, so the sum of the script's time does not set the load; what runs between two steps does. Nothing here measured which of a page's tasks are on the chain.

Tests. build\test_all.exe -Quick -NoAsan: every step passes. WPT, against wpt/expectations: css/css-nesting 24 tests, css/css-shadow 91, html/semantics/scripting-1 470, html/webappapis/scripting/processing-model-2 53, dom/nodes 379: no regression. css/css-contain and css/selectors are not in the checkout (wpt/suites.txt), so container queries have the unit tests alone. The series above ran before container_conds_lost, which only takes a saving back.

Not verified. The release build, a long session, the full WPT, the full test262, AddressSanitizer: not run. No other work was seen on the machine during the series; that was not checked at each load.

#What changed, round 49: what a restyle marks for nothing, and what the load follows

Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load, base (3da0459f) kept apart, arms interleaved, the order turning. Temporary code, none in the tree: a tally of what marked each element restyled and what it cost, by rule and by cause, the style threads off so that one thread counts; ids on the loop's tasks with who posted them; a sleep after each task of the window thread; layout's reasons. Public sites.

Why the elements restyled on cnn.com changed nothing. One load of the base, one thread: 11 815 elements restyled, match 365 ms, cascade 87, comparison 20. Matching is 77 % of a restyle, so a no-change element cannot be made cheap past the cascade: a record of what went into a style, to skip it, would have taken a fifth. What marked them:

elementschanged
forced by a parent: --scrollbar-width and --page-width written on <html>, every element's custom properties4 7694 769
any reach of a positional compound: a <script> added to <body> or to a wrapper looked at every sibling for :last-child .x, then under eachabout 3 0000
:not(:has(~ [data-component-name="stack"])): read alone, the :has() was an anchor on any elementabout 2 000a few
the rest (a class rewritten with the same tokens under [class*=...], real class changes, what was inserted)about 2 000the other 380 or so

(Rounded, from two loads and the tally's rows.) Of what is marked rather than forced, 95 % changes nothing, as round 48 said; the 44 % that change in all are the ones forced, which the walk finds by comparing and no invalidation decides. And two rules out of 5 443 held 92 of 340 ms of matching: .layout-homepage-mobile :is(.container, ...):has(+ :not(...)) and its neighbour, 120 us an answer. Tried 587 000 times in all, 50 an element, and 440 more turned down by the ancestor filter.

1. :first-child, :last-child, :only-child are read at the ends of a list (edge_first, edge_last, edges_changed; :nth-child(1) too). What is first now, or stood first before this batch: that one is the first child that did not come in this batch, whatever came before it, so one look per parent per batch instead of a walk of the siblings from the place of the change. In a list nothing left and with nothing new at its end, nothing. restyle_dom_edges_are_read_at_the_edges; restyle_dom_random has these rules now.

2. A :has() in a :not(), :is(), :where() is anchored by the compound around it (Has_Anchor.around). .a:not(:has(.b)): the element is an .a; the compound in the :not() said nothing, so every ancestor of every change was an anchor, whose reach was then scanned for its subject's keys. A :not() holding a chain stands for another element and keeps nothing. restyle_dom_has_anchor_in_a_not_is_the_compound_around_it.

3. :has(+ .a) tries the next element, :has(~ .a) the siblings (matches_has_scan). Each answer went through every following sibling and all it held; only a descendant combinator in the argument goes under them, only ~ or a sibling combinator before it goes past the next one. Restyle_Stats.has_steps, restyle_dom_has_siblings_looks_where_the_argument_can_be.

After them, the same load: 9 163 restyled, 4 800 of them the forced ones, match 259 ms with the tally's own cost, 453 000 tries.

What the load follows: all of the window thread, at a slope of 1. A task on theverge.com's last wait is a script whose life is mostly waiting. Walking back from the load event by who requested and posted what, one load, ms:

hoprequestedreached the pagecompileturnran
bounce's i.js6581 23816501 403
runtime1 4041 6960-in a task of 149
btloader1 5562 03170182 119, 30 ms
ads-v22 1482 7072433733 323, 4 ms
a timer, 12 ms late3 338, 24 ms
jquery3 3393 5751903 594, 7 ms, load at 3 600

The tasks of the chain ran 302 ms of 3 400; their own work is nothing. ads-v2's last byte came 15 ms after its request and reached the page 559 ms later. Another load ended on recaptcha's frame, the next on metrics/3OJ5...: several chains, none the same twice. Those waits are the queue: in 3 450 ms of frames up to the load the thread waited for 68. 1 239 ms of timers, 1 045 of scripts, 285 of promise jobs after a response, 147 + 117 of posted tasks and ports, 237 of animation frames. #What changed, round 51: whose work the window thread does, and no scheduler

host.run_ready ran tasks that said who posted them and nothing of whom they were for. Now every posted task and timer has a base.Work: the page, the origin of the script behind it, a class (Arrival: parsing and what arrives for it; Input: input and paint; Background: timers and the rest). A task or a timer inherits from what makes it (Loop.work, host.work_now), so an origin follows a script's timers, its responses (fetch.Task.work), its listeners, its animation frames and idle callbacks. js_run says the origin of the script it runs; the pump, a document's bytes and a response open a host.work_enter scope. The engine does not say which script a function came from: a function of one script called from another's task counts for the latter. What a class is a call site says; the pump's timers, image pumps and events, sheets' syncs are Arrival though they are timers: a timer is not a class, and a scheduler that went by the queue they sit in would have put the parser's own turns behind the ads.

WREN_SPANS writes class, page, origin and party on Task and Work rows; wrentool threadtime <files> gives each instant of the window thread to the innermost owner, a frame's phases outside a task to the browser's Input, a frame's wait to nobody. Windows: from the navigation to the first contentful paint, to the last largest contentful paint, to settled (the first end of work after the load event followed by 500 ms with under 10 % busy; SETTLE_*). wrentool waterfall -AfterMs n lets a page run on for it. Busy time is the thread's wall clock, not its CPU.

What it says. Development build, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load, 10 s after the load event, the sites interleaved, 3 runs, median (range), ms. No scheduler was built, on these numbers. The proposal was parser, script arrival and paint ahead of third-party timers while a document loads.

  • Ready. Third-party timers ran 0 to 1 ms before the first contentful paint on all four sites, and 0, 19, 0 and 0 ms before the largest. That is the whole of what moving them could give a paint, at the slope of 1 of round 49: nothing, or 19 ms on a page whose largest paint ranges over 960 ms. The scripts that set them have not arrived yet at that moment, or have only just.
  • Settled. Reordering removes no work. A thread settles when its work is done, and the timers run anyway, so at best settled stays. That leaves only the load event to move, which is the scheduler this brief forbids and what round 48 saw of a body handed over sooner.
  • What the turn does already. run_ready runs all posted tasks before any timer, and timers for a slice of 8 ms at most past the first: arrivals, compile results and responses already go first. All that could be added is the order among due timers.
  • npr.org's 473 ms before the largest paint are no timer: a checkpoint run as a task (host_post_checkpoint), promise jobs of the page's own script, which it needs.

So a built scheduler would have had to be tested for starvation and for cnn.com's 940 to 18 200 ms (docs/blocker.md: a heavy script let through before the first frame) to buy a measured 0 to 19 ms. The ceiling was computed, not measured by a build, as in round 47: the sums above are what ran, and no run of a held-back timer was made.

If it is ever built, what HTML allows. Checked in the specification, not assumed. A user agent chooses among task queues freely ("chosen in an implementation-defined manner"), and its example is input preferred three quarters of the time without starving the others, but one task source is never processed out of order. Timers: the timer task source, "wait a further implementation-defined length of time" is allowed, and the wait of run steps after a timeout holds per global and ordering identifier: a timer waits for those started before it with an equal or shorter timeout. So the unit is the global, not the origin: two timers of one window keep their order whichever script set them, and a third-party script's timer cannot be passed by a later first-party one in the same window with an equal or longer timeout. Only a whole global, a third party's frame, can be held behind another; host.Timer.work.page is what that needs. Work.third_party alone would break the rule.

Where the numbers point instead. Nothing here is a scheduling cause. Before the first paint, on the three heavy sites, the thread is on the paint's own path: Input and first-party Arrival are 200 to 375 of 238 to 496 busy ms. theverge.com's third-party Arrival before the paint went from 12 to 133 ms between runs and is the one thing there that a paint could wait for (not looked into). Up to settled what is left is less work: frames first (19 to 45 % of the thread on the heavy sites), then concert.io, OneTrust and recaptcha's frame, each with a name now.

Owners cost nothing that shows: base and round, no spans, 6 runs interleaved, the order turning, first contentful paint / load / CPU to the load: cnn.com 591 (556-931) / 4 042 (3 703-5 361) / 7 953 (7 250-9 297) against 589 (542-1 346) / 3 887 (3 659-8 458) / 7 500 (7 062-15 500); theverge.com 418 (405-616) / 6 255 (6 153-8 010) / 10 062 (9 578-12 203) against 402 (388-497) / 6 148 (5 812-7 931) / 9 656 (8 844-11 375). Ranges overlap: nothing to claim either way.

The origin of a callback is who registered it as far as a scope said so; promise jobs count for whoever runs the checkpoint. third_party compares sites, and a company's own CDN counts as a third party. Workers have owners on their own loops, which the report does not read. The ceiling assumes a paint can only gain what ran before it on the thread.

#What changed, round 52: what an element matched, kept

Development builds, wrentool waterfall -Runs 1, a fresh process and a throwaway profile for each load. Temporary code, none in the tree: a tally of the elements each kind of pass matched and the time the matching took (summed over the style threads), and switches that turn each item off in the same binary, which is what the base below is. Other work ran on the machine all along: the times are of a loaded machine, the counts are not.

The ceiling first. One load each, base: elements restyled for what they inherit alone, matched all the same, and what their matching took:

forced by a parent (restyle_dom)a container's size (restyle_containers)shadow trees
cnn.com9 232, 571 ms1 217, 64 msnone
npr.org22 340, 63 msnone
theverge.com43 533, 22 msnone
bbc.com/news04none

It pays on cnn.com, and on the container walks of the others.

1. What an element matched is kept, and a pass whose cause is inheritance alone reuses it (matched.odin). A selector never reads a computed style: an element forced by its parent, or under a container whose size moved, matches what it matched, and only the cascade runs again. A list per element (Styled.matched, by slot, a pointer), the lists kept once each in the engine (Matched_Store, hash consing on rule and selector, outliving a Styled: the next full pass finds them). A stale list is ruled out by where it is written and read, not by invalidations:

  • it is written where matching happens (compute_element), for every element matched by any pass, whatever its record does next;
  • it is read only for an element no mark names (Frame.whole, M_SELF; Pass.unmarked for the container walk, which requires the styles to be of the document as it is). Every pass that may change what an element matches (mutations, states, @media, sheets that come or go) marks what it reaches and so matches it again;
  • the lists point at rules: engine_rebuild ends them all (Matched_Store.gen); a Styled of another generation reads and writes none;
  • @container conditions, hints and the style attribute are not in a list: the cascade reads them each time;
  • a document with a shadow tree has no lists (matched_holds): which tree's rules an element sees follows the flat tree. None of the four sites has one;
  • verify_styles compares every list with a full pass's, so every restyle test checks them (restyle_dom_random now writes a custom property on its root in a tenth of its steps), and so does style.incremental.verify on a page: the 4 sites twice, 669 partial passes after DOM changes, @media flips and sheets, no difference.

Memory: the lists of cnn.com are 717 for 13 000 elements, 170 KB, and the slots 8 bytes each, 105 KB: 3.7 % of its 7.4 MB of styles. npr.org 130 + 123 KB, theverge.com 174 + 51, bbc.com/news 37 + 15. A store past 16 MB keeps no new list and starts over at the next full pass (MATCHED_MAX_BYTES). Taken a load: cnn.com 10 464 to 11 699 elements, 3.5 to 3.9 ms for all of them; npr.org 2 342, theverge.com 4 441 to 4 884. matched_an_inherited_change_matches_nothing, matched_every_kind_of_pass_keeps_the_list, matched_go_with_the_rules, matched_lists_are_shared, matched_past_the_limit_matching_runs, matched_shadow_trees_match.

2. An attribute selector is asked of the old value and the new (Inv_Index.attr_tests). [class*=x] .y reached its subtree at any change of class, a class rewritten with the same tokens too; now only when its answer flips. Pseudo-classes read from attributes (:any-link) keep what they reach (attr_other). Past ATTR_TESTS_MAX (256) selectors of one name, the union as before: cnn.com has 85 of class. restyle_dom_attribute_selectors_read_old_and_new. Not measured apart.

3. :nth-child(3) and :nth-last-child(-n + 2) are read from the end of the list, as :first-child (nth_edge_depth, edges_changed). An element whose index was or is b has fewer than b elements before it that did not come in the batch: what stands past the first b of them, and before the first that came or the place of the first that left, kept its index. On theverge.com an element added at the end of a list walked back over all its siblings for :nth-last-child(2): elements restyled by restyle_dom before the load 3 344 to 1 334 (medians), the walk back 2 820 to 28. Read first as "something left this parent", it quadrupled cnn.com's (4 170 to 16 000): a removal anywhere restyled the first three children of <body> with what they hold. The place of each removal is in the journal (Lost_Place). restyle_dom_nth_near_the_edge; restyle_dom_random has these rules now.

#What changed, round 53: a smaller heap, for a shorter collection

No thread, no barrier: fewer and smaller cells, so that the marking has less to visit and the sweep less to free. Development builds; base 4753a790 (build/js_base), the round's engine passed to the same wren.exe with WREN_JS_IMAGE, compiled code from the disk cache (WREN_TEST_WASM_CACHE) for both. Public sites; other agents were at work on the machine.

The measure. -define:JSRT_GC_CENSUS=true counts each cell the sweep frees, by the rows of the heap's census (memprof.odin: census_cell, Runtime.gc_dead); Runtime.gc_swept counts cells freed and kept in every build (the census's swept row). WREN_JS_MEMPROF=1 now prints the census of a window's realm at its load event too (js_census_at_load), with what died (DEAD rows) from such an engine. A temporary change, not in the tree, also counted each cell made by (native function, function of the script), and each field of Cell and Object in use. Counts of one load; a page does not run the same work twice, so the census says what a load is made of, the page loads below say what it costs.

Read by what made them: 94 % of the function expressions that died had their prototype made, and dead with them: 408 k of the plain objects of theverge.com, 243 k of npr.org's. Half the objects (1.37 M of 2.7 M on theverge.com) had their slots in a block of their own: every array, closure, arguments object. 145 k mapped arguments objects on theverge.com, 83 k array iterators, 61 k for-in iterators. Of npr.org's strings, 2.4 M are made in one callback of OneTrust's otBannerSdk.js, legIntVendors.findIndex(e => e.includes(t.toString() + ":true") || ...): the same number made a string twice per element; 576 k in OtAutoBlock.js's replace of each URL, needed. OneTrust's otTCF.js makes about 800 k cells on each of the three pages, babel's _objectSpread2 and ownKeys (Object.keys, getOwnPropertySymbols, filter, forEach): what the language asks, arrays that are new each time. The fields: Cell.ext (references the host holds) is not zero in 1.5 % of the live cells and never over 65 535 (two cells over 255 on theverge.com); pinned, in_ext and the kind's flags are bits; a native's magic was in each object's union. The sizes on wasm32, what ships: Cell 16, Object 52 (plain: 116 with its 4 slots, unaligned), string header 36, Var_Ref 48, Object_Data 20, an iterator's state 152 in a block of its own.

1. The header and the objects (gc.odin, object.odin). Cell is 8 bytes: the kind in a nibble beside pinned, in_ext and two bits of the kind's own, mark a byte, the host's count in 16 bits, which sticks at its top (the cell is then a root for good: a cell, not a correctness). Object 40: a native's magic in the object (Object.magic), so Native_Data is 12 and the union 16. String header 28, Var_Ref 32 (detached when pvalue points at its own value: var_ref_is_detached). #asserted on wasm32. Measured, not kept: the same 8 bytes as a bit_field of 32 bits with a 22-bit count made the engine's code 430 KiB larger and each read of a kind a shift and a mask; a byte for mark and a nibble for the kind cost 27 KiB.

2. One block per object (object_new_shape, object_tail, array_like_new). Slots follow the object in its cell whenever it is made with them (an empty plain object has room for 4; one of a known shape, exactly its keys: an iterator's result is 72 bytes, was 116). After them, what lives as long as the object: a closure's cells, an iterator's state, the values of an array, an arguments object or a match made with their room (Object.keys, map, slice, an array literal, the JIT's too). What grows past it takes a block of its own, and the cell's room stays unused. An iterator of an array, a map, a string or a for-in carries 64 bytes of state, its helpers' and regexps' 84 more after it (Iter_Extra).

3. A function's prototype when first used (Prop_Kind.lazy_prototype, function_prototype_make). The slot stays empty and the property's kind says so; what reads, defines or describes it makes the object and moves the function to the shape the same keys have as data; F.prototype = ... makes nothing first (function_prototype_settle). The fast paths of the interpreter and of the JIT take only .data; the others go by the kind, and switch on it is exhaustive.

4. The strings of numbers (str_from_u64). The last string of each of 256 slots by value, cleared by each collection: t.toString() for each element of a list is one string.

5. The sweep (gc_sweep_step). A cell that owns nothing but its block (a plain object with its slots inline, a flat string, a closure cell) is freed without a finalizer (cell_alone), into the free list at once; the heap is charged once a step.

What each case of cost.js costs, Wasm instructions an iteration, interpreted (fuel; collections included), base -> round: a function expression 2 808 -> 1 898, an arrow function 2 185 -> 1 986, new Promise 5 882 -> 5 622, a number made a string again 2 497 -> 2 075, a map's entries by next() 5 349 -> 4 729, destructured pairs 5 036 -> 4 854, arguments of a sloppy function 3 303 -> 3 204, {a, b, c} 1 625 -> 1 616; slice of 8 4 332 -> 4 246, concat 7 947 -> 7 882, filter 15 134 -> 15 058, forEach the same. realworld.js under jsengine mem: 100 -> 87 collections, the module's linear memory 65.4 -> 48.8 MB. A fresh realm: JS heap 1 469 -> 1 351 KiB, linear memory 6 848 -> 6 592 KiB; the image 9 377 -> 9 328 KB.

Left, by what was seen. Mapped arguments (145 k a load on theverge.com) make a closure cell for each mapped parameter: an arguments object that reads the frame while it lives, copied at its return, would make none. A for...of or a destructuring of a plain array makes an iterator object nothing sees (83 k a load); the operand stack could hold the array and an index. A Value of 8 bytes is the large one left (another round measures its ceiling).

Tests. hotcheck.js (passes in Node): a function's prototype reached every way (read, new, instanceof, a descriptor, defineProperty, Reflect.set, an assignment, delete, freeze, a dictionary shape, keys in order before and after keys of its own, a generator's eager one); slots, closure cells, arguments and match values past what their cell holds; destructuring, map iterators kept open, for-in. cost.js: three new cases, and the limits of the closures and of new Promise brought down to a tenth over the round. Under -define:JSRT_GC_STRESS=8192 -define:JSRT_GC_POISON=true: hotcheck.js, jitcheck.js (also verify -jit -jit-threshold 1), objectspread.js, realworld.js, recursion.js pass. test262 on the native judge, all of it: 43 233 of 43 267, the same 34 failures as before.

#Round 56: a replay bench, and what it can prove

Two arms of one binary differed by 180 ms on cnn.com in wrentool waterfall (round 48): a public site changes its requests with its ads and a run changes with the network, so a gain of 1 to 5 % could not be told from nothing. This round builds the bench that can, and uses it for three measures. No engine optimization; the 32-byte Value of measure 3 was a temporary patch, gone.

The bench (testing). wrentool replay record keeps what a site served for one load (src/net/record.odin, one file per answer under build/replay/<site>, out of git); run serves those bytes from wrentool's own process (tools/testserver/replay.go) to a page with a seeded random and a clock of its own (src/base/test_world.odin: WREN_TEST_WORLD, which a release never reads). Every name reaches the server by network.hosts=*=127.0.0.1:<port> (new: one line sends every connection to one address, whatever its name and port), each certificate comes from the test authority (network.tls.extra_ca_file), network.loopback_only keeps the load on the machine: neither the hosts file nor the trust store is touched. Per load: visually ready (the first frame from which the first viewport stays within 0.5 % of its last picture, carousels left out by a rule), settled (the window thread idle for 500 ms after the load event, idle being at most 25 % on a processor) and CPU to settled (the window thread's cycle counter, read from outside it), with FCP, load, DOMContentLoaded, CPU and Guest to the load event beside them. A gain is visually ready or settled sooner with the ranges apart and CPU to settled no worse (measure.verdict); work moved past an event says Moved.

What building it found.

  • A redirect never comes to its end: the browser follows it from its head and cancels the request. The first recording of cnn.com had no document (www.cnn.com answers 301): a redirect is recorded from its head now.
  • The page's clock, at 0.1 ms a read, saw 0.1 s of a 4 s load of cnn.com (1 000 reads): a script that yields after so many ms never would. At 2 ms a read cnn.com sees 1.4 s of 3.3, npr.org 4.9 s of 9 (page_clock), and the number of reads is the same from one load to the next to 0.5 % on cnn.com, 3 % on npr.org: the same work.
  • cnn.com and theverge.com never go idle. Once their work is done the window thread stays 15 to 20 % busy for as long as they are open (frames and timers of their own, one sample a second over 20 s), npr.org and bbc.com/news go below 5 %. Hence the 25 % of settled.
  • The copy of each frame costs the window thread about a ms: on a page that draws all the time, recording the frames alone kept the thread from ever looking idle, and moved CPU to the load by 6 %. The frames come from a second load of each run, up to the moment the first one settled.
  • The machine is shared. During this round other agents and test runs kept it at 20 to 100 % for hours; theverge.com's load went from 3.5 s to 11. A load now starts when at most a fifth of the processors are at work, and one during which the rest of the machine took more than 35 % (others) is dropped and made again.

The noise floor. Two arms of one binary (wren_base.exe twice), 7 runs each after one warm-up, the order turning, frames on; the other agents' work took 8 to 35 % of the machine during the loads (others). Per metric, the distance of the two medians, then the floor of measure.noise_floor (the larger of that distance and of how far one run strays from its median), % of the median:

Read plainly. The medians of 7 agree to 0 to 2.5 % on the three primary metrics, on every site; a single run strays 4 to 37 %. So a series of 7 tells a change of about 3 % in its medians, and proves one of 5 to 10 % with the ranges apart, on this machine as it was: not 1 %. FCP and DOMContentLoaded are ten times shorter and stray most. bbc.com/news has one mode now, where round 46 saw two (450 ms or 2 s): the modes were the network.

Why it stays noisy: the machine, not the page. The page does the same work. Its clock reads, which follow every branch a script takes, are the same from load to load to 1 % on cnn.com (1 382 to 1 394 ms of page clock at 2 ms a read, one load at 1 422), 3 to 5 % on npr.org, theverge.com and bbc.com/news (three values there: 1 905, 2 003, 2 095), and so are the requests (cnn.com 160 or 161, all exact). What moves is how long the same work takes, and it moves with the rest of the machine: cnn.com's CPU to settled is 2 891 to 2 980 ms in the six loads where others took at most 19 % of the processors, 3 043 to 3 308 in the eight where they took 22 to 32 %; npr.org 7 554 and 7 795 at 8 and 10 %, 8 302 to 9 252 above 19 %. The cycle counter counts time on a processor, which a neighbour on the other half of a core or in the shared cache makes longer. theverge.com adds one of its own: settled is a threshold, and its tail of timers after the load either leaves a window of 500 ms idle at 4.3 to 4.7 s or not until 5.3 to 6.4 (two groups, both arms). On a quiet machine the floor would be the first group's: about 3 % on cnn.com's CPU to settled, in six runs.

1. What the filter lists change. wrentool waterfall forced blocker.update.enabled=false on a throwaway profile: every measure until now ran on the built-in list. A user has, about 15 s after a first start, not two lists but the ten on by default (blocker/conf.odin: EasyList, EasyPrivacy, AdGuard Base, the five of uBlock, Peter Lowe's, URLhaus; 22 MB of text, an engine of 35 MB): wrentool replay lists fetched them once, and run -Lists puts them in the profile. Read plainly. Of what we have been optimizing, a user with the lists runs a fraction: theverge.com's Guest to the load event 94 ms of 2 595 (4 %), its CPU to the load 12 %; npr.org's Guest 59 %, cnn.com's 112 % (the lists block fewer requests there; why its script costs more with them was not looked into), bbc.com/news 46 %. By CPU to settled, the measure that cannot be moved past an event: theverge.com 51 % of the built-in list's, npr.org 76 %, cnn.com 103 %, bbc.com/news 104 %. And every first contentful paint comes 440 to 590 ms later with the lists, DOMContentLoaded with it: by the look of it the first navigation after a start waits for the engine of 35 MB, which the built-in list does not have (process_cpu 1 s more on cnn.com; not traced). That is the cost a user pays at each start of the browser, measured here at each run because each run is a start; a page after the first does not pay it, and that was not measured. On bbc.com/news the lists bring the load event sooner and settled later: a Moved by the rule.

The bench should default to the lists, two arms or one: measuring with the built-in list optimizes work most users never run (three quarters of theverge.com's script), and misses what they do (the engine's start, cnn.com's cosmetic filters). Not done in this round: -Lists is a flag, the folder has to be fetched first (wrentool replay lists), and the default of a bench should move with the round that takes it up. The first-paint cost at start-up is the largest single thing on the table here, ahead of anything the engine could give these pages.

Doubling Value costs theverge.com 8 % of Guest and 6.4 % of the window thread's CPU to the load, bbc.com/news 9.5 and 8.4 %, ranges apart; npr.org 2.5 and 1.3 %, cnn.com 4.9 and 0.3 %, ranges overlapping. The engine is a third of cnn.com's thread (round 46: its imports are style and layout), which is why it moves least. An upward slope only suggests the downward one: 8 bytes would save the copies and half the cache lines of the operand stack, the locals and the properties, and add what a NaN-boxed value costs to tag and untag at each operation, which 32 bytes never paid. Read it as "the size of a value is worth up to about 5 to 10 % of Guest on script-heavy pages", not as what 8 bytes would give.

3. The Wasm tax. The same script work on the engine compiled natively (judge eval, src/engine/jsrt/judge, -o:speed -debug, the engine's own allocator on the system heap) and through the shipped image (jsengine run, Wasmtime, the image's polls), interpreter only and with the JIT (-jit, which translates hot functions to Wasm); the same file in both, console.log shimmed to print. examples/jsbench micro, macro and realworld (55 cases, ns per iteration), and the 40 largest scripts of the four recordings, compiled and not run (new Function of the text: run without a DOM, a page's script reaches the web API, which the image traps on and the judge has not), interleaved, best of 3 rounds:

Read plainly. Through Wasm the interpreter takes 1.46 times the native time, geometric mean of 55 cases (1.14 for a loop of numbers, 1.2 to 1.3 for properties, 1.4 to 1.6 for calls, allocation and collections, 1.7 to 2.1 for regular expressions, strings and JSON), and compiling the pages' scripts 1.59 times. That is the ceiling of a native engine on the window thread, before what it would cost to have one (the sandbox, a second engine for workers). With the JIT the tight loops run 20 to 50 times faster than the native interpreter, and what allocates, compiles a regexp or calls natives gains nothing; a load runs almost nothing in compiled code (round 46: 2 samples of 2 266 on theverge.com), so the JIT's column says little of a page. Limits: the judge is the engine with the judge's host (no browser imports, Date.now from the system), so a page's calls into the browser, 10 to 43 % of Guest (round 46), are not in it; jsbench measures the interpreter's own cases, not a page's mix; the machine was shared (as above), which moves both arms alike in each pair but not the absolute times.

Found on the way: the judge built -o:speed without -debug runs a plain loop 10 times slower (50 million s += i: 14.9 and 15.4 s, against 1.46 and 1.40 s with -debug, the same flags otherwise). Its profile then has no names, so where was not looked for; wrentool engine test262 and the CI build the judge their own way, which was not checked. Every number above is of the -debug build.

Measured, built, not kept.

  • settled at 5 % of the thread in 250 ms (the first rule): cnn.com and theverge.com never settled within 20 s (their floor of 15 to 20 %), and npr.org did one load in three.
  • The frames in the measured load: the copy of each frame on the window thread kept npr.org from settling at all and added 6 % to its CPU to the load; they are in a second load now.
  • A guard that waited for 8 % of the machine: in five hours of other agents' work it found almost no window at all.

Left, by what was seen. The engine's start with the lists (440 to 590 ms of every first paint after a start) is the largest thing measured here. Then the lists' cost on cnn.com's script (Guest +12 % with the lists against the built-in one), not looked into. The bench: a quiet machine, or a measure robust to a neighbour (a process of its own on reserved cores, or the counts of what a load did, which the page clock shows are stable, rather than its time); theverge.com's settled in two groups; TEST_WORLD_TICK_MS chosen by two sites. The noise floor above is the one to beat: a change of a few percent needs more than 7 runs or a quieter machine.

Tests. src/tools/wrentool/measure/measure_test.odin (settled after the load and not before, a short gap, a frame loop that never settles, ready against the last picture, a fade, a carousel left out, the floor, the verdict), tools/testserver/replay_test.go (order, the near answer, a 404 counted, TLS and plain http on one port over HTTP/2, a rewind, the head served less what is of the hop, a folder that is no recording), src/tools/e2e/replay_bench.odin (any name through network.hosts=* to the recording with its certificate, the same seed giving the same Math.random, getRandomValues and randomUUID twice and another seed others, a cookie of the recording's date kept, the page's year, a clock that moves by its reads, the unknown script counted; and a load recorded as the host was given it, its body decoded), the resolver's * line in native/net (Rust). build\test_all.exe -Quick -NoAsan on the final tree: 211 steps pass, 1 cached. A run before it, with the machine loaded, failed the documentation site (not yet generated), the lines of text decoration by their pixels and WPT's text-decoration-thickness-interpolation.html; those two passed alone on the same tree.

Not verified. The release build (the test world and the recorder are out of it by WREN_CHANNEL, not run), Linux (base.thread_cycles is 0 there and the bench is a Windows tool), a long session, the full WPT, test262, AddressSanitizer. The noise floor on a quiet machine: none was had. Whether a page under the test world behaves as it does in real time beyond the counts above (its timers keep real time while its clock moves by reads). Recordings are of one load each, on 2026-11-07: a site's next version is another recording.

#Inventory

#Internal caches (remove by making the path fast; product caches kept)

Kept, a product: the HTTP cache (src/httpcache), the back/forward cache (browser/bfcache.odin), compiled scripts on disk (js/cache.odin), compiled Wasm modules (wasm/module_cache.odin), the Cache API (page/cache_store.odin): each saves the network or a compiler's work across navigations and starts, which no faster path can. GPU residency, not caches: the glyph atlas (font/raster.odin:71), Slug glyph data (font/slug_cache.odin:44), image textures (browser/images_shell.odin:70), retained pictures (browser/compositor.odin:129, with its memory budget). Not a cache either: the table of a style pass that gives elements with the same inputs the same computed style (style/share.odin, round 4): it holds the values that pass made and goes with it, nothing in it is invalidated; nor the families of the walk that share matching between alike elements (style/sibling_match.odin, round 5): what the pass matched for the first of a kind, dropped when the walk leaves that family; nor the pairs of records a chunk of the layout journal's comparison has compared (style/journal.odin, round 8), which live while that chunk is compared.

#Hash tables on hot paths

style/engine.odin:68-69 (by_id, by_class, by_tag, by_attr: string keys looked up per class, id, tag and attribute of every element, plus a concatenation per indexed attribute at cascade.odin:577); style/match.odin:58-67; style/cascade.odin:476-493 (custom properties, contexts, fs_chain per element); layout/context.odin:28-58 (anon_cs, frame_cs; font_cache gone in round 4); layout/types.odin:479 (scroll, read per space); browser/compositor.odin:114 (node_items, a heap list per node) and :419-554 (per rebuild); page/images.odin css_images_sync and page/fonts.odin fonts_sync (a seen table of shared lists, now only when something new may be used); ext/gui_toolkit/font/raster.odin:77-82 (per glyph, under the atlas lock); page/timeline.odin et_seen (per element with elementtiming only). Gone in round 1: page/timeline_lcp.odin ls_prev (per box, per mutated frame). Added in round 4, flat: style/share.odin (a style pass's shared styles: open addressing, the keys' words in one array, one lookup per element). Gone in round 5: style/restyle_dom.odin inserted_exceed (the inserted nodes of a restyle, now bits by handle index). Gone in round 7: the glue's node handle -> wrapper table (native/js/odin/wj/qjs_platform.odin, now an array by handle index; the hash table holds only the handles whose entry is taken, none on nodes10k). Gone in round 9: layout/multicol.odin mc_records (a container's columns, looked up for each box and line of its flow; now an array, Box.mc the index).
